intro.en: Comprehensive pharmacology and practical examination review of 49 essential drugs in obstetrics and gynaecology, detailing indications, clinical regimens, dosages, adverse reactions, contraindications, and viva questions.

items.summary: A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used for rapid blood pressure reduction in pre-eclampsia and as a first-line oral tocolytic in preterm labour.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Belongs to the dihydropyridine class of calcium channel antagonists.
Commercial trade preparations include Depin and Nicardia.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by the oral route.
Sublingual route is documented historically but is clinically contraindicated.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Directly dilates peripheral arterioles by blocking inward calcium flux, decreasing systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure.
Inhibits voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels in myometrial cells, suppressing smooth muscle contractility to produce tocolysis.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Antihypertensive: 5-10 mg bd/tds, maximum 120-160 mg.
Tocolytic: 20-30 mg orally, and continued every 3-8 hours as 20 mg until contractions subside. Used for a maximum of 48 hours. The maximum dose is 160 mg over 24 hours.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Acute tocolytic suppression of contractions in preterm labour.
Tocolysis to suppress uterine hypercontractility associated with fetal compromise.
Temporary cessation of uterine activity to facilitate completion of antenatal corticosteroids.
Tocolysis to allow safe in utero transfer of the mother to a tertiary neonatal unit.
Antihypertensive therapy in pre-eclampsia and chronic gestational hypertension.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal hypotension and peripheral vasodilatation.
Reflex maternal tachycardia accompanied by palpitations.
Nausea and vomiting.
Cutaneous facial flushing.
Throbbing vascular headache and lightheadedness or dizziness.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Maternal structural cardiac pathology due to heightened hazard of pulmonary oedema.
Caution warranted in multiple pregnancy because of increased pulmonary oedema vulnerability.
Diabetes mellitus requires careful supervision due to risk of pulmonary oedema.
Significant hepatic dysfunction.
Simultaneous administration with beta-sympathomimetics or magnesium sulphate due to synergistic cardiovascular depression.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Demonstrates superior tocolytic efficacy and safety relative to beta-sympathomimetics and magnesium sulphate.
Sublingual delivery must be strictly avoided as it precipitates dangerous rapid maternal hypotension and placental hypoperfusion.

viva.q: Why is sublingual nifedipine avoided in obstetric hypertensive emergencies?
viva.a: Sublingual administration causes an abrupt, uncontrolled fall in maternal arterial pressure, precipitating reflex tachycardia and critical reduction in uteroplacental blood flow.

viva.q: What is the maximum duration and daily ceiling dose of nifedipine when prescribed for tocolysis?
viva.a: The maximum duration of tocolytic therapy is 48 hours, and the cumulative ceiling dose must not exceed 160 mg over 24 hours.

image.brief: Blister strip containing 10 mg nifedipine soft capsules positioned next to a blister pack of 20 mg sustained-release tablets on a clean neutral grey backdrop.

items.summary: A combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist used as a first-line agent for acute and maintenance control of pregnancy hypertension.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Antihypertensive drug combining selective alpha-1 antagonism with non-selective beta-adrenergic blockade.
Commercial market preparations include Labebet and Gravidol.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally for maintenance control.
Given intravenously for acute hypertensive emergencies.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Highly selective antagonist at post-junctional alpha-1 receptors while non-selectively blocking beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors.
Relaxes vascular smooth muscle and lowers systemic vascular resistance, reducing blood pressure without provoking severe reflex tachycardia.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral: 100 mg-200 mg OD to QDS, maximum 2400 mg/day.
IV: 20 mg -> 40 mg -> 80 mg -> 80 mg, maximum 220 mg in hypertensive emergencies.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Urgent lowering of arterial blood pressure in severe pre-eclampsia.
Control of acute severe hypertension in eclampsia.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Postural hypotension and orthostatic lightheadedness.
Dizziness, drowsiness, and profound fatigue.
Nausea and epigastric discomfort.
Frontal headache.
Bronchospasm and exertional dyspnoea.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Second- or third-degree atrioventricular heart block.
Decompensated congestive cardiac failure.
Pre-existing severe hypotension or cardiogenic shock.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or active bronchial asthma.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker contraindicated in asthma, cardiac failure, renal impairment, and diabetes because it causes severe bradycardia and hypotension.

viva.q: Outline the intravenous dosing schedule for labetalol in acute hypertensive crisis of pre-eclampsia.
viva.a: Start with 20 mg slow IV; double the dose to 40 mg after 10 minutes if target blood pressure is unmet, then 80 mg, and 80 mg, up to a maximum of 220 mg.

viva.q: Why is labetalol contraindicated in women with asthma?
viva.a: Its non-selective beta-2 receptor antagonist activity promotes bronchoconstriction, which can precipitate life-threatening acute bronchospasm.

image.brief: Clear glass 4 mL ampoule of labetalol hydrochloride 5 mg/mL (20 mg total) displayed beside a blister strip of 100 mg oral tablets on a flat white surface.

items.summary: A direct-acting arteriolar vasodilator employed intravenously for acute blood pressure control in severe pre-eclampsia and eclamptic emergencies.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Direct-acting peripheral arteriolar vasodilator.
Marketed under trade brand formulations such as Apresonile.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by oral administration.
Administered by slow intravenous bolus injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Selectively relaxes vascular smooth muscle in precapillary resistance arterioles without affecting capacitance venules.
Decreases total systemic peripheral resistance, leading to a prompt reduction in maternal arterial blood pressure.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral: 100 mg od-qds.
IV: 5-10 mg IV -> 5-10 mg repeated in 30 minutes, maximum 20 mg.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Acute therapeutic reduction of blood pressure in severe pre-eclampsia.
Parenteral blood pressure control during hypertensive crises of eclampsia.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Prominent reflex tachycardia and distressing palpitations.
Severe throbbing frontal headache and facial cutaneous flushing.
Excessive precipitous maternal hypotension.
Gastrointestinal disturbances including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea.
Drug-induced lupus erythematosus-like syndrome on extended therapy.
Haematological suppression including leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and agranulocytosis.
Peripheral oedema, cardiovascular collapse, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatomegaly with jaundice.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe resting sinus tachycardia.
Congestive cardiac failure and right ventricular hypertrophy or failure.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Myocardial insufficiency secondary to severe valvular heart disease.
Dissecting aortic aneurysm.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What is the primary hemodynamic mechanism of hydralazine?
viva.a: It exerts direct relaxation on arteriolar smooth muscle, reducing systemic vascular resistance with negligible effect on venous capacitance beds.

viva.q: State the intravenous administration protocol and maximum dose for hydralazine in severe pre-eclampsia.
viva.a: Administer 5-10 mg slow IV bolus; if blood pressure remains elevated after 30 minutes, repeat 5-10 mg IV, up to a cumulative limit of 20 mg.

image.brief: Sterile glass ampoule containing 20 mg/mL hydralazine hydrochloride solution positioned beside a reconstitution vial on a smooth white clinical surface.

items.summary: A centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic agonist with extensive safety data, used for non-emergency management of chronic and gestational hypertension in pregnancy.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Centrally acting sympatholytic antihypertensive agent.
Brand trade names include Alpha Dopa, Methyl Dopa, and Gynapres.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally for standard maintenance therapy.
Intravenous infusion may be employed in acute hypertensive crisis.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Metabolised centrally to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, which stimulates inhibitory central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem.
Reduces central sympathetic outflow to peripheral blood vessels, lowering vascular resistance and mean blood pressure.
Suppresses circulating plasma renin activity and produces mild peripheral arteriolar vasodilation.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral: 250-500 mg OD-QDS, maximum 3 g/day.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Maintenance antihypertensive therapy for chronic and pregnancy-induced hypertension during the antenatal gestation.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Nausea and vomiting.
Sinus bradycardia and postural hypotension with dizziness.
Marked central nervous system sedation, somnolence, and lethargy.
Haemolytic anaemia mediated by warm autoantibodies, associated with a positive direct Coombs test.
Thrombocytopenia and drug-induced lupus erythematosus-like syndrome.
Maternal mental depression and severe exacerbation of postpartum depression.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Postpartum period due to high propensity to induce or aggravate postnatal depression.
Active psychiatric conditions or prior history of endogenous depression.
Congestive cardiac failure (CCF).
Active hepatic disorders or chronic liver cirrhosis.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: Why is alpha methyldopa contraindicated in the immediate postpartum period?
viva.a: It depletes central biogenic amines and readily precipitates or worsens severe maternal postpartum depression.

viva.q: Which distinctive haematological test becomes positive during long-term methyldopa therapy?
viva.a: The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which can be accompanied by autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

image.brief: Blister strip of circular 250 mg film-coated yellow alpha methyldopa tablets laid flat on a clean white clinical background.

items.summary: An essential parenteral mineral salt that serves as the gold-standard anticonvulsant in eclampsia and provides neuroprotection against cerebral palsy in very preterm births.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Inorganic electrolyte anticonvulsant, membrane stabiliser, neuroprotective agent, and osmotic laxative.
Commonly termed Epsom salt; pharmaceutical preparations include Magneon and Lubic.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by deep intramuscular injection.
Administered by controlled intravenous infusion or slow bolus injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Depresses central nervous system irritability and blocks motor end-plate acetylcholine release, dampening neuromuscular transmission.
Inhibits peripheral and cerebral convulsions and alleviates cerebral oedema by stabilising neuronal membranes.
Promotes intraluminal colonic water retention when given orally, stimulating peristalsis and bowel evacuation.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Pritchard loading dose: 4 gm i.v over 10-15 minutes, then 10 gm i.m (5 gm in each buttock).
Pritchard maintenance dose: 5 gm i.m in alternate buttocks every 4 hours until 24 hours after delivery or last fit.
Zuspan regimen: 4 gm i.v over 10-15 minutes -> 1 gm per hour as infusion until 24 hours after the last fit or 24 hours after delivery, whichever is later.
Recurrent convulsions: 2 gm MgSO4 i.v.
Cerebral palsy neuroprotection: 4 gm i.v over 10-15 minutes -> 1 gm per hour as infusion for 24 hours before delivery in preterm birth under 30 weeks.
Sibai regimen: 6 gm MgSO4 -> over 20 minutes -> 2 gm as IV infusion.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prophylaxis and treatment of convulsions in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.
Fetal neuroprotection to prevent cerebral palsy in anticipated delivery prior to 30 weeks gestation.
Intravenous replacement therapy in maternal hypomagnesaemia.
Osmotic reduction of oedema in third-degree uterine procidentia using a topical glycerine and magnesium sulphate compress.
Saline osmotic laxative for rapid bowel evacuation.
Adjunctive bronchodilator in acute refractory status asthmaticus.
Second-line tocolytic agent in preterm labour.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Peripheral flushing, sensation of warmth, drowsiness, and hypotension.
Visual disturbances including diplopia and blurring.
Metabolic derangements: hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and hyperkalaemia.
Respiratory depression, intercostal muscle paralysis, and respiratory arrest.
Neurological toxicity at serum magnesium over 5 mmol/L: loss of patellar reflexes, facial paraesthesia, and muscle paralysis.
Cardiac toxicity at serum magnesium over 7 mmol/L: profound bradycardia, complete atrioventricular block, and circulatory arrest.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known drug hypersensitivity.
Pre-existing hypermagnesaemia.
Severe hypercalcaemia.
Pre-existing myocardial structural injuries or advanced atrioventricular block.
Diabetic coma.

blocks.title: Monitoring and antidote
bullets: Therapeutic serum magnesium level: 2-3.5 mmol/L (4-7 mEq/L or 5-9 mg/L).
Loss of deep tendon patellar reflexes occurs at levels exceeding 3.5 mmol/L (>7 mEq/L or >9 mg/L).
Respiratory muscle paralysis occurs at levels exceeding 5 mmol/L (>10 mEq/L or >12 mg/L).
Cardiac arrest occurs at levels exceeding 12.5 mmol/L (>25 mEq/L or >30 mg/L).
Mandatory monitoring parameters: respiratory rate, arterial oxygen saturation, deep tendon knee reflexes, and hourly urine output.
If knee jerk is lost with preserved respiration, halt magnesium sulphate and measure serum electrolyte levels.
If respiratory rate falls, discontinue magnesium sulphate, administer oxygen, and give 10% calcium gluconate as 10 ml over 10 minutes as IV.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Cochrane review evidence demonstrates magnesium sulphate significantly lowers maternal mortality and recurrent fits compared to diazepam, phenytoin, or lytic cocktail.
Infants born following maternal magnesium sulphate experience fewer low Apgar scores and shorter hospital stays than those exposed to diazepam.
Lytic cocktail regimen consists of pethidine 100 mg and chlorpromazine 25 mg in 20 mL of 5% dextrose as IV, with chlorpromazine 50 mg and promethazine 25 mg as IM.

viva.q: What three clinical parameters must be verified prior to administering each maintenance dose of magnesium sulphate?
viva.a: Presence of the patellar knee reflex, a maternal respiratory rate of at least 16 breaths per minute, and urine output of at least 30 mL per hour.

viva.q: What is the specific pharmacological antidote and dosage for magnesium sulphate toxicity?
viva.a: 10% calcium gluconate, administered as 10 mL intravenously over 10 minutes.

viva.q: At what serum magnesium concentrations do knee jerks disappear and respiratory paralysis supervene?
viva.a: Knee reflexes disappear when serum levels exceed 3.5 mmol/L (7 mEq/L), while respiratory paralysis develops at levels above 5 mmol/L (10 mEq/L).

image.brief: Pair of clear glass 50% magnesium sulphate ampoules (1 g/2 mL each) placed beside a 10 mL ampoule of 10% calcium gluconate on a clean surgical field.

items.summary: An ultra-short-acting, light-sensitive parenteral vasodilator reserved for refractory, life-threatening hypertensive crises unresponsive to standard therapies.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Potent, direct-acting nitric oxide-releasing mixed arterial and venous vasodilator.
Commences hypotensive activity within 2 minutes of starting parenteral administration.
Trade names include Nipride, Nitropress, and Nipress.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Exclusively administered as an intravenous infusion.
Direct intravenous bolus injection is strictly prohibited.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Spontaneously generates nitric oxide in circulating blood, relaxing vascular smooth muscle.
Reduces both cardiac preload and afterload by dilating arterial and venous beds.
Dilates coronary vascular channels.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Anti-hypertensive: 0.25-0.3 microgram/kg/min iv infusion, increasing by increments of 0.5 microgram/kg/min IV infusion tailored to individual response.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Emergency control of severe refractory hypertension unresponsive to conventional drugs.
Management of acute congestive cardiac failure.
Treatment of acute left ventricular pump failure.
Alleviation of severe cerebral vasospasm.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal: Hypotension, tachycardia, palpitations, cardiac arrhythmias, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, restlessness, confusion, oliguria, and metabolic acidosis.
Maternal toxicity: Azotaemia, methaemoglobinaemia, cyanide poisoning, and thiocyanate accumulation.
Fetal and neonatal effects: Oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), neonatal renal failure, and transplacental cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Acute cardiac failure associated with reduced peripheral vascular resistance.
Hypertension associated with aortic coarctation or an arteriovenous shunt.
Hepatic dysfunction.
Severe renal impairment.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Must be infused continuously via a dedicated pump; direct intravenous push is contraindicated.
Oral intake is lethal because nitroprusside is converted to toxic free cyanide.
Adverse toxic features stem primarily from accumulation of liberated cyanide ions.
Cyanide toxicity is reversed by infusing sodium thiosulphate, generating thiocyanate that is safely eliminated in urine.
Infusion apparatus must be wrapped in opaque protective foil; solution must be discarded if discolouration occurs.

viva.q: Why must an intravenous infusion of sodium nitroprusside be protected from light exposure?
viva.a: Photochemical degradation rapidly breaks down the molecule, causing accelerated release of toxic cyanide ions into the circulation.

viva.q: What is the specific therapeutic antidote for acute cyanide poisoning caused by sodium nitroprusside?
viva.a: Intravenous sodium thiosulphate infusion, which converts toxic cyanide into less toxic thiocyanate for excretion by the kidneys.

image.brief: Amber glass vial containing 50 mg sodium nitroprusside powder wrapped in protective light-excluding foil beside an intravenous infusion giving set on a plain surface.

items.summary: An organic nitrate vasodilator used for acute blood pressure control in pre-eclampsia, management of cardiac ischaemia, and rapid intrapartum uterine relaxation.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Organic nitrate producing powerful venodilation and arteriolar smooth muscle relaxation.
Commercial formulations include Nitrosol, Glyceryl trinitrate, and Nitro-Bid.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Delivered by continuous intravenous infusion.
Administered via the sublingual route.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Acts on venous capacitance beds to cause predominant venodilatation, lowering cardiac preload.
Relaxes vascular smooth muscle via enzymatic nitric oxide generation, decreasing both preload and afterload.
Improves collateral myocardial blood flow and lowers systemic arterial blood pressure.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Antihypertensive: Initial infusion of 5 micrograms/minute, titrating upward every 3-5 minutes by increments of 5-20 micrograms/minute, up to a maximum of 100 micrograms/minute.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Antihypertensive therapy in severe pre-eclampsia.
Management of hypertensive crises.
Rapid tocolytic agent for acute uterine relaxation during obstetric emergencies.
Medical management of maternal angina pectoris.
Induction of controlled intra-operative hypotension during surgery.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal hypotension and compensatory reflex tachycardia with palpitations.
Facial flushing, nausea, and vomiting.
Pulsatile headache and dizziness or lightheadedness.
Blurring of vision and acute syncopal episodes.
Methaemoglobinaemia, contact dermatitis, rebound hypertension, and thrombocytopenia.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Traumatic head injury or suspected cerebral haemorrhage.
Hypertensive or hepatic encephalopathy.
Hepatic dysfunction and severe renal impairment.
Narrow-angle glaucoma.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Severe throbbing headache represents the most frequent adverse reaction reported by patients.

viva.q: Name two obstetric emergencies where sublingual or intravenous nitroglycerine is employed for tocolysis.
viva.a: Acute uterine inversion to facilitate manual repositioning of the fundus, and trapped aftercoming head of a breech presentation during vaginal delivery.

viva.q: What is the single most common maternal complaint during nitroglycerine infusion?
viva.a: Severe throbbing vascular headache resulting from rapid cranial meningeal vessel vasodilatation.

image.brief: Amber glass dropper bottle of 0.5 mg sublingual glyceryl trinitrate tablets resting next to a 5 mL ampoule of 5 mg/mL nitroglycerine solution on a neutral backdrop.

items.summary: Antihypertensive agents used in non-pregnant individuals but strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to severe fetotoxicity and the oligohydramnios sequence.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Inhibitors of angiotensin-converting enzyme.
Representative agents include Naprilate (Enalapril), Ritemed (Captopril), and Ramipro (Ramipril).
Strictly avoided in pregnancy because of proven severe teratogenicity.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by the oral route.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Inhibits the enzyme converting angiotensin I into active vasoconstrictor angiotensin II.
Reduces angiotensin II levels, suppressing adrenal aldosterone synthesis and blunting sodium and fluid retention.
Relaxes arteriolar and venous smooth muscle via nitric oxide generation, decreasing both cardiac preload and afterload.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Antihypertensive (in non-pregnant patients):
Captopril: 25-50 mg BD/TDS.
Enalapril: 2.5-5 mg OD.
Lisinopril: 5 mg OD.
Ramipril: 1.25 mg OD.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Strictly contraindicated throughout all trimesters of pregnancy.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal effects: Hypotension, tachycardia, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, flushing, headache, dizziness, persistent dry non-productive cough, angioedema, dysgeusia, and maculopapular rash.

Fetal and neonatal effects: Oligohydramnios, neonatal calvarial hypoplasia, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures, fetal growth restriction (IUGR), fetal renal tubular dysgenesis, and fatal neonatal anuria.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pregnancy (absolute contraindication in all stages).
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: Why are ACE inhibitors absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy?
viva.a: They provoke severe fetal renal tubular dysgenesis, profound oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures, and neonatal renal failure.

viva.q: What causes the characteristic chronic cough associated with ACE inhibitors?
viva.a: Inhibition of ACE halts the enzymatic degradation of bradykinin and substance P in bronchial airways, triggering cough receptor stimulation.

image.brief: Blister strips of 5 mg enalapril tablets and 2.5 mg ramipril capsules placed together with prominent warning labelling against pregnancy on a white surface.

items.summary: Medications that enhance renal excretion of water and electrolytes, reserved in pregnancy for pulmonary oedema, heart failure, and massive fluid overload.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Pharmacological agents promoting urinary excretion of water and electrolytes.
Includes loop diuretics (Frusemide-Lasix), thiazides (Chlorthiazide-Diuril, Bendrofluazide, Chlorthalidone), and potassium-sparing diuretics (Spironolactone).

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral administration.
Intramuscular injection.
Intravenous injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Loop diuretics (Frusemide): Block sodium and potassium absorption in the thick ascending limb of Henle; superior diuretic potency to thiazides.
Thiazides (Chlorthiazide, Bendrofluazide, Chlorthalidone): Inhibit sodium and potassium reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Potassium-sparing agents (Spironolactone): Competitively antagonise aldosterone receptors in collecting tubules.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Pregnancy-induced hypertension complicated by massive generalized oedema.
Severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia complicated by acute pulmonary oedema.
Severe maternal anaemia in pregnancy presenting with congestive cardiac failure.
Adjunctive therapy with direct vasodilators like hydralazine to prevent reflex fluid retention.
Prophylactic administration immediately prior to blood transfusion in severe anaemia to avert circulatory overload.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Loop diuretics: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, muscular weakness, and maternal hypotension.
Thiazides: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, maternal hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, acute pancreatitis, polyuria, and glycosuria.
Spironolactone: Feminisation and incomplete androgenisation in the male fetus due to anti-androgenic effects.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Contract maternal plasma volume and thus generally avoided in routine uncomplicated pregnancy to protect uteroplacental perfusion.
Contraindicated during lactation because drug passes into breast milk and can trigger neonatal volume contraction and dehydration.

viva.q: What is the primary maternal indication for intravenous furosemide in pre-eclampsia?
viva.a: Acute pulmonary oedema secondary to left ventricular dysfunction or fluid overload in severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia.

viva.q: Why are diuretics avoided in standard non-oedematous pre-eclampsia?
viva.a: Pre-eclampsia is already associated with reduced maternal intravascular volume; diuretics cause further volume contraction and compromise placental perfusion.

image.brief: Pair of 2 mL clear glass ampoules of frusemide 20 mg/2 mL for injection beside a blister card of 40 mg oral tablets on a light medical work surface.

items.summary: A first-generation hydantoin anticonvulsant used for generalized and focal seizures, occasionally employed as a reserve agent in refractory eclampsia.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: First-generation anti-epileptic hydantoin derivative and centrally acting anticonvulsant.
Formulated under commercial brand names including Eptoin and Epsolin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally for chronic epilepsy.
Administered by intravenous injection or infusion.
Intramuscular route is technically available but poorly absorbed.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Blocks voltage-gated neuronal sodium channels, prolonging their inactivated state.
Inhibits sustained repetitive firing of action potentials, curbing spread of abnormal seizure foci.
Reduces presynaptic neurotransmitter exocytosis and inhibits calcium flux at high concentrations.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: In eclampsia: 10 mg/kg body weight -> 5 mg/kg after 2 hours.
Ryan loading dose: 15 mg/kg body weight IV (10 mg/kg initially over 30 minutes, then 5 mg/kg 2 hours later over 10 minutes).
Ryan maintenance dose: 300 mg IV over 10 minutes, given until 24 hours have passed since the last seizure.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Maintenance anticonvulsant for generalised tonic-clonic seizures and focal seizures.
Intravenous management of status epilepticus.
Second-line management of convulsions in eclampsia when magnesium sulphate is contraindicated.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Neurological: Cerebellar ataxia, horizontal nystagmus, diplopia, and cognitive impairment.
Endocrine and metabolic: Inhibits insulin release causing hyperglycaemia, and suppresses antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion.
Dermatological and connective: Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Haematological and systemic: Megaloblastic anaemia, coagulopathy, neutropenia, leukopenia, and drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe cardiac conduction defects including sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial block, and atrioventricular block.
Pregnancy due to teratogenicity, unless benefits clearly outweigh risks in refractory epilepsy.
Lactation.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Fetal hydantoin syndrome craniofacial signs: Short palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, flat midface, low nasal bridge, thin upper lip, micrognathia, cleft lip, and cleft palate.
Fetal hydantoin syndrome systemic signs: Congenital heart defects, growth and mental deficiency, and hypoplastic distal digits with underdeveloped nails.
Intravenous infusion rate must not exceed 50 mg/min to avoid acute cardiovascular collapse and fatal arrhythmias.
Must be infused slowly or administered via controlled intravenous infusion diluted only with normal saline.

viva.q: What is the maximum permissible intravenous infusion rate for phenytoin and why?
viva.a: 50 mg/minute; exceeding this infusion rate can trigger severe hypotension, complete heart block, and fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

viva.q: Name three classical dysmorphic facial and digital features of fetal hydantoin syndrome.
viva.a: Cleft lip or palate, depressed nasal bridge with epicanthal folds, and hypoplasia of distal phalanges with rudimentary nails.

image.brief: Vial of 100 mg/2 mL phenytoin sodium solution next to a blister strip of 100 mg oral tablets on a neutral grey background.

items.summary: A long-acting benzodiazepine providing muscle relaxation, sedation, and rapid anticonvulsant activity in acute seizure emergencies.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Long-acting benzodiazepine acting as an anticonvulsant, central skeletal muscle relaxant, and anxiolytic.
Commercially prepared under brand names including Valium and Calmpose.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral tablets.
Intravenous injection.
Intramuscular injection.
Per rectal administration.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Modulates post-synaptic GABA-A receptor transmission, increasing presynaptic inhibition.
Acts selectively upon the limbic system, thalamus, and hypothalamus to exert calming, sedative, and anticonvulsant effects.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: General intravenous dose: 2-10 mg IV in general, up to a maximum of 30 mg.
Preoperative preparation, ICU sedation, or endoscopy: 5-10 mg IV.
Status eclampticus: 5-10 mg IV, can repeat in 5-10 minutes if seizures persist.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Pre-operative sedation.
Procedural sedation administered 30 minutes prior to endoscopy to calm and relax the patient.
Anxiolytic therapy for acute panic states.
Emergency management of general seizure disorders.
Anticonvulsant therapy for acute eclampsia where magnesium sulphate is unavailable.
Arrest of prolonged status epilepticus.
Symptomatic relief of severe acute muscle spasm.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal: Hypotension, headache, dizziness, euphoria, motor incoordination, somnolence, cutaneous rash, diarrhoea, fatigue, respiratory depression, depression, and blurred vision.
Fetal and neonatal: Marked neonatal hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome) and respiratory depression.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known drug hypersensitivity.
Acute alcohol intoxication.
Myasthenia gravis.
Glaucoma.
Severe pre-existing respiratory depression.
Comatose states.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Avoid administration just before delivery and during lactation due to neonatal accumulation.
Cochrane review proves magnesium sulphate is associated with significantly less mortality and fewer recurrent seizures than diazepam in eclampsia.
Fewer newborns exhibit low Apgar scores at delivery when magnesium sulphate is used instead of diazepam.
Hospital stay is significantly shorter with magnesium sulphate than diazepam.
Magnesium sulphate is substantially superior to diazepam, phenytoin, and lytic cocktail regimens in eclampsia.

viva.q: Why is magnesium sulphate preferred over diazepam in controlling eclamptic fits?
viva.a: Cochrane review evidence shows magnesium sulphate significantly reduces maternal mortality, prevents recurrent seizures, and prevents neonatal hypotonia and low Apgar scores.

viva.q: What neonatal complication arises if diazepam is administered immediately before birth?
viva.a: Floppy infant syndrome, manifesting as severe neonatal hypotonia, hypothermia, reluctance to feed, and respiratory depression.

image.brief: Amber glass ampoule of 10 mg/2 mL diazepam injection beside a blister card of 5 mg tablets on a sterile white work surface.

items.summary: An intermediate-acting benzodiazepine anticonvulsant and anxiolytic used for procedural sedation and status eclampticus.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Intermediate-acting benzodiazepine possessing anticonvulsant and anxiolytic properties.
Marketed commercially as Lopam and Larpose.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral ingestion.
Intravenous injection.
Intramuscular injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Enhances central GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission, increasing membrane chloride conductance.
Produces central nervous system depression, raising the threshold for epileptic discharges.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Anticonvulsant in status eclampticus: 4 mg per dose as slow IV over 2 minutes; if a seizure persists, repeat 4 mg IV.
Anxiolytic: Loading dose 0.02-0.04 mg/kg, maintenance dose 0.01-0.1 mg/kg, maximum 10 mg/hour as IV.
Preoperative sedative: 0.05 mg/kg, 2 hours before surgery.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Pre-operative sedative prior to major surgical interventions.
Procedural anxiolysis administered 30 minutes prior to endoscopy to calm and relax the patient.
Short-term treatment of severe acute anxiety.
Arrest of convulsions in active seizure disorders.
Second-line anticonvulsant therapy in eclampsia.
Acute abortive therapy in refractory status epilepticus.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal central effects: Fatigue, headache, dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, sedation, asthenia, ataxia, disorientation, amnesia, vertigo, and dysarthria.
Maternal systemic effects: Nausea, vomiting, flushing, visual blurring, hypotension, respiratory depression, extrapyramidal symptoms, convulsions, and jaundice.
Fetal and neonatal: Marked muscular hypotonia, respiratory depression, and the gasping fetus syndrome.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known drug hypersensitivity.
Narrow-angle glaucoma.
Accidental or direct intra-arterial administration.
Severe pre-existing respiratory depression.
Obstructive sleep apnoea.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Not recommended for breastfeeding or lactating mothers.
Should never be administered immediately prior to delivery because it provokes floppy infant syndrome in the newborn.

viva.q: What is the recommended intravenous dose and delivery rate of lorazepam in status eclampticus?
viva.a: 4 mg given as a slow intravenous injection over 2 minutes; this may be repeated once after several minutes if convulsions persist.

viva.q: Why is direct intra-arterial injection of lorazepam strictly contraindicated?
viva.a: Intra-arterial injection induces intense arterial vasospasm, vessel thrombosis, distal gangrene, and potential loss of the affected limb.

image.brief: Clear glass vial containing 2 mg/mL lorazepam injection beside a blister card of 2 mg scored tablets on a clean neutral background.

items.summary: A long-acting synthetic ergot derivative and dopamine D2 receptor agonist used for hyperprolactinaemia, prolactinomas, and puerperal lactation suppression.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic ergot alkaloid derivative exhibiting potent, selective dopamine D2 receptor agonist activity.
Proprietary formulations include Cabgolin and Caberlin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered exclusively by the oral route.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Directly activates dopamine D2 receptors located on anterior pituitary lactotroph cells.
Strongly inhibits synthesis and exocytotic release of prolactin into systemic circulation.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Standard oral therapeutic regimen: 0.25-0.5 mg twice a week.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical management and tumour shrinkage of pituitary microprolactinomas and macroprolactinomas.
Induction of ovulation in anovulatory infertility secondary to hyperprolactinaemia.
Treatment of persistent galactorrhoea associated with prolactinoma.
Elective lactation suppression following late intrauterine fetal demise.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Common: Nausea, vascular headache, postural dizziness, and constipation.
Uncommon: Abdominal pain, blurred vision, breast pain, peripheral oedema, palpitations, cardiac arrhythmias, dyspepsia, depression, fatigue, hypotension, and psychiatric disturbances.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe uncontrolled arterial hypertension.
Severe pre-eclampsia.
Known hypersensitivity to ergot derivatives.
Pre-existing structural cardiac or valvular fibrotic disorders.
Severe hepatic impairment.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Induces an approximate 80% reduction in prolactinoma tumor size.
Successfully restores ovulatory cycles in up to 95% of treated women.
Echocardiography (ECHO) is recommended every 6-12 months during long-term therapy to monitor for fibrotic cardiac valvular insufficiency.

viva.q: Why is regular echocardiographic monitoring advised for patients receiving chronic cabergoline therapy?
viva.a: Long-term ergot-derivative exposure can stimulate 5-HT2B serotonin receptors on heart valves, leading to fibrotic cardiac valvular regurgitation.

viva.q: What is the typical dosage schedule of cabergoline in the treatment of hyperprolactinaemic anovulation?
viva.a: 0.25 to 0.5 mg administered orally twice per week.

image.brief: Blister packaging showing small circular 0.5 mg scored white cabergoline tablets on a clean neutral grey backdrop.

items.summary: An oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant used in non-pregnant states and select mechanical heart valves, but avoided in early pregnancy due to embryopathy.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Oral synthetic dicoumarol derivative and vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant.
Trade preparations include Uniwarfin, Warf, and Sofarin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Interferes with hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as endogenous regulatory protein C and protein S.
Depletes functional active vitamin K stores, blunting post-translational gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Primary prophylaxis against deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary thromboembolism.
Treatment of established venous thromboembolism.
Thromboprophylaxis in pregnant women with mechanical prosthetic heart valves between 12 and 36 weeks gestation.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Warfarin embryopathy: Nasal hypoplasia, congenital heart defects, ventriculomegaly, agenesis of corpus callosum, stippled epiphysis, small phalanges and limbs, and chondral calcification.
Fatal fetal intracerebral haemorrhage.
Intrauterine fetal demise and stillbirth.
Spontaneous maternal haemorrhage, severe postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), and extensive perineal haematoma.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pregnancy (especially first trimester and near term), except in select women with high-risk mechanical prosthetic heart valves.
Known bleeding diathesis.
Threatened miscarriage.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: International normalised ratio (INR) should be maintained in between 1.5-2.0.
If essential in pregnancy, start after 12 weeks up to 36 weeks; during remaining periods, LMWH or unfractionated heparin should be substituted.
The antidote for warfarin is vitamin K. Severe overdose is treated with prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) and fresh frozen plasma (FFP) along with vitamin K.

viva.q: What specific anatomical defects constitute classic warfarin embryopathy?
viva.a: Nasal hypoplasia with depressed bridge, chondrodysplasia punctata (stippled epiphyses), shortened limbs with hypoplastic distal digits, and agenesis of the corpus callosum.

viva.q: What is the recommended anticoagulation strategy for a pregnant patient with a mechanical heart valve taking warfarin?
viva.a: Substitute LMWH or UFH during the first 12 weeks to avert embryopathy, give warfarin from 12 to 36 weeks, and switch back to heparin after 36 weeks.

image.brief: Blister strip of 5 mg circular pink warfarin tablets positioned beside a clinical international normalised ratio (INR) monitoring log on a white desk.

items.summary: The gold-standard parenteral anticoagulant in pregnancy and the puerperium, offering predictable bioavailability, no placental passage, and low bleeding risk.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Fractionated low molecular weight heparin anticoagulant.
Common trade brand formulations include Clexane, Lupenox, and Maxiparine.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: LMWH: Administered by subcutaneous injection.
Unfractionated heparin (UH): Administered by intravenous or subcutaneous injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Potentiates antithrombin III, accelerating inactivation of activated factor Xa and clotting proteases.
Possesses a high ratio of anti-factor Xa to anti-factor IIa (thrombin) activity.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Weight-adjusted dosing schedules:
Under 50 kg: Enoxaparin 40 mg BD/60 mg OD; Dalteparin 5000 IU BD/10000 IU OD; Tinzaparin 175 units/kg OD.
50 kg to 69 kg: Enoxaparin 60 mg BD/90 mg OD; Dalteparin 6000 IU BD/12000 IU OD.
70 kg to 89 kg: Enoxaparin 80 mg BD/120 mg OD; Dalteparin 8000 IU BD/16000 IU OD.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prophylaxis of antenatal and postnatal venous thromboembolism in high-risk women.
Therapeutic management of acute deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in pregnancy.
Management of thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome in combination with low-dose aspirin.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Accelerated bone mineral density loss and osteoporosis with prolonged therapy.
Systemic allergic reactions and cutaneous hypersensitivity.
Local bruising, hematoma, and pain at subcutaneous injection sites.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known bleeding disorders such as haemophilia or von Willebrand disease.
Active antepartum or postpartum haemorrhage.
Severe hepatic disease and severe renal insufficiency.
Severe uncontrolled arterial hypertension.
Thrombocytopenia with platelet count less than 75000 cells/cmm.
Haemorrhagic stroke or ischaemic stroke within the preceding 4 weeks.
Women diagnosed with major placenta praevia.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: LMWH versus UFH: LMWH is preferred in pregnancy, does not cross placenta, has no teratogenic effects, and does not require routine anti-Xa monitoring.
UFH crosses placenta, is teratogenic, requires INR/aPTT monitoring, and carries higher risk of osteoporosis and bleeding.
Maternal platelet counts should be monitored every 2-3 days postpartum.
LMWH elimination half-life is 4-5 hours (compared to 1-2 hours for UFH); has no complete antidote, whereas protamine sulphate reverses UFH.
Regional neuroaxial anaesthesia requires a minimum interval of 12 hours after a prophylactic dose of LMWH (versus 4 hours for UFH).
Aspirin 75 mg OD (low-dose aspirin) is used for pre-eclampsia prevention (CLASP study), recurrent pregnancy loss, FGR, and thrombophilia.

viva.q: Why is LMWH preferred over unfractionated heparin for thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy?
viva.a: LMWH does not cross the placenta, has superior bioavailability and longer half-life, requires no routine laboratory monitoring, and carries lower risks of bleeding and osteoporosis.

viva.q: What is the mandatory waiting period between prophylactic LMWH and regional spinal anaesthesia?
viva.a: A mandatory interval of at least 12 hours is required following a prophylactic dose before administering regional neuroaxial anaesthesia.

image.brief: Pre-filled glass syringe of enoxaparin 40 mg/0.4 mL with integral safety needle shield beside an unboxed carton on a clean medical tray.

items.summary: A fluorinated corticosteroid administered to mothers at risk of preterm delivery to accelerate fetal pulmonary maturity and reduce neonatal mortality.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic fluorinated glucocorticoid steroid.
Commercial injectable brand formulation includes Betnesol.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by intramuscular injection for fetal lung maturity.
Oral and intravenous routes exist for other medical indications.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Accelerates morphological maturation of alveolar type 1 and type 2 pneumocytes.
Induces synthesis of surfactant apoproteins and critical enzymes for phospholipid formation, improving pulmonary mechanics and compliance.
Decreases microvascular endothelial permeability and advances structural maturation of fetal lungs.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: For fetal lung maturity: 12 mg I.M, 2 doses given 24 hours apart.
Alternative dexamethasone regimen: 6 mg, 4 doses given 12 hours apart.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Antenatal prophylaxis in all women at risk of imminent preterm labour prior to 34 to 36 weeks gestation.
Prophylactic course prior to elective caesarean section (LSCS) before 39 + 0 weeks to prevent transient neonatal respiratory morbidity.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: A single clinical course produces minimal adverse maternal or neonatal effects.
Transient maternal hyperglycaemia may occur, requiring adjusted insulin coverage in diabetic gravidas.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active maternal systemic sepsis.
Uncontrolled active systemic tuberculosis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Significantly reduces neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).
Reduces incidence of necrotising enterocolitis (NEC).
Reduces neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH).
Significantly decreases neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions.
Optimal clinical efficacy begins 24 hours after the second dose and persists up to one week.
Can be administered in diabetic women following admission, with close maternal blood glucose monitoring.

viva.q: What is the standard antenatal betamethasone dosing protocol to induce fetal lung maturity?
viva.a: 12 mg administered intramuscularly as two separate doses given 24 hours apart.

viva.q: Enumerate four significant neonatal complications reduced by antenatal corticosteroid administration.
viva.a: Respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis, and neonatal intensive care unit admissions.

image.brief: Two 2 mL clear glass ampoules of betamethasone sodium phosphate injection (4 mg/mL) placed next to an intramuscular syringe on a white sterile tray.

items.summary: Sympathetic beta-2 receptor agonists used historically for acute tocolysis to permit antenatal steroid completion, but limited by maternal cardiopulmonary adverse effects.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Sympathomimetic agents that stimulate beta-adrenergic receptors, mimicking adrenaline and noradrenaline.
Common examples include Salbutamol, Terbutaline, Isoxsuprine, and Ritodrine.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered via oral, intravenous, subcutaneous, and inhalational routes.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Directly stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, activating adenylate cyclase and increasing intracellular cyclic AMP.
Reduces intracellular free calcium concentrations, suppressing actin and myosin interaction and causing myometrial smooth muscle relaxation.
Acts as a tocolytic by relaxing uterine smooth muscle, and as a bronchodilator by relaxing bronchiole smooth muscle.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Short-term tocolytic therapy to arrest contractions and enable completion of a full corticosteroid course.
Tocolysis to facilitate maternal in utero transfer to a tertiary facility.
Uterine relaxation prior to performing external cephalic version (ECV).
Acute tocolytic relief of fetal distress caused by a hyperstimulated uterus.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal: Tachycardia, palpitations, hypotension due to vascular smooth muscle relaxation, flushing, sweating, headache, tremors, and anxiety.

Maternal metabolic/pulmonary: Hyperglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia, hypokalaemia, lactic acidosis, pulmonary oedema, cardiac arrhythmias, angina, cardiac failure, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Fetal and neonatal: Fetal tachycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac failure, intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD), neonatal hypoglycaemia, and neonatal hypotension.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Maternal organic heart disease.
Severe hypertension or severe hypotension.
Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism.
Antepartum haemorrhage, as uterine arterial dilation can exacerbate bleeding.
Diabetes mellitus warrants extreme caution due to severe ketoacidosis risk.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Not widely preferred in modern obstetrics because safer tocolytic alternatives such as nifedipine and atosiban are available.

viva.q: Why is antepartum haemorrhage a major contraindication to beta-sympathomimetic tocolytics?
viva.a: Beta-2 mediated vascular smooth muscle relaxation dilates uterine arteries and can precipitate massive, catastrophic maternal haemorrhage.

viva.q: What characteristic maternal metabolic disturbances are provoked by intravenous beta-agonists?
viva.a: Severe hyperglycaemia resulting from hepatic glycogenolysis, hypokalaemia from intracellular potassium shifting, and lactic acidosis.

image.brief: Glass ampoule of ritodrine hydrochloride 10 mg/mL injection positioned next to a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler on a plain clinic work surface.

items.summary: A competitive oxytocin and vasopressin V1a receptor antagonist used as a targeted parenteral tocolytic with minimal maternal cardiovascular side effects.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic cyclic peptide acting as a competitive oxytocin receptor antagonist.
Also blocks vasopressin V1a receptors in the myometrium.
Marketed internationally under trade names including Tractocile.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered strictly by intravenous injection and continuous infusion.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively blocks myometrial oxytocin receptors, preventing oxytocin-induced inositol triphosphate generation.
Decreases intracellular free calcium release and reduces extracellular calcium influx, producing uterine relaxation.
Suppresses oxytocin-stimulated local release of prostaglandins PGE and PGF2-alpha.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Bolus dose: 6.75 mg IV over 1 minute.
Maintenance infusion: 18 mg IV/hour for 3 hours, then 6 mg/hour for 45 hours.
Maximum cumulative dose: 330 mg over the full treatment course.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Acute tocolytic suppression of uncomplicated preterm labour between 24 and 33 completed weeks.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal nausea and vomiting.
Transient headache.
Infrequent maternal chest discomfort or pain.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: General obstetric conditions where tocolysis is contraindicated: severe pre-eclampsia, chorioamnionitis, and antepartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Largely displaced beta-sympathomimetics in high-resource centres due to its favourable maternal cardiac safety profile.
Significant clinical limitation is its high procurement cost compared with oral nifedipine.
Lacks maternal cardiovascular contraindications, unlike beta-agonists and nifedipine.

viva.q: What is the pharmacological mechanism of action of atosiban?
viva.a: It acts as a competitive antagonist at myometrial oxytocin and vasopressin receptors, inhibiting calcium influx and halting oxytocin-mediated prostaglandin release.

viva.q: Outline the three-stage intravenous administration regimen for atosiban.
viva.a: Initial 6.75 mg IV bolus over 1 minute, followed by 18 mg/hour infusion for 3 hours, then 6 mg/hour for 45 hours, not exceeding 330 mg total.

image.brief: Glass vial of atosiban acetate 6.75 mg/0.9 mL bolus injection resting beside a 5 mL concentrate vial for infusion on a sterile surgical tray.

items.summary: A non-selective cyclo-oxygenase inhibitor used for short-term tocolysis before 32 weeks and for the medical reduction of symptomatic polyhydramnios.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and non-selective cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibitor.
Trade formulations include Indmecin, Indoflam, and Indopar.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Non-selectively inhibits cyclo-oxygenase enzymes, halting arachidonic acid conversion into uterine prostaglandins.
Lowers intracellular free calcium in myometrial myocytes, attenuating actin-myosin coupling and suppressing contractions.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: In polyhydramnios: 25 mg TDS-QDS orally.
In preterm labour: Loading dose of 50-100 mg orally or rectally, then 25 mg QDS orally for 48 hours.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Short-term tocolysis to suppress contractions in acute preterm labour.
Analgesic relief for acute inflammatory pain.
Medical reduction of excess amniotic fluid volume in severe polyhydramnios.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal effects: Gastritis, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, overt gastrointestinal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, asthma exacerbation, and renal impairment.
Fetal and neonatal effects: Oligohydramnios, premature constriction or closure of the ductus arteriosus, necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), and intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH).

viva.q: Why is indomethacin tocolysis restricted to gestational ages below 32 weeks and durations under 48 hours?
viva.a: Prolonged exposure or use beyond 32 weeks markedly increases the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure, pulmonary hypertension, and neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.

viva.q: What mechanism allows indomethacin to reduce amniotic fluid volume in polyhydramnios?
viva.a: It reduces fetal renal blood flow and urinary output while enhancing fluid reabsorption across fetal pulmonary membranes.

image.brief: Blister strip of 25 mg opaque green indomethacin capsules lying next to an intact box on a grey clinical surface.

items.summary: A posterior pituitary nonapeptide hormone used for induction and augmentation of labour, active management of the third stage, and prevention of postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Endogenous nonapeptide neurohypophyseal hormone synthesised in the supraoptic and paraventricular hypothalamic nuclei.
Synthetic pharmaceutical equivalents include Syntocinon and Pitocin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by intravenous infusion for labour induction and augmentation.
Administered by intramuscular injection for active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL).

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Binds to specific G-protein-coupled oxytocin receptors on myometrial cell membranes.
Triggers calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum and stimulates rhythmic, coordinated uterine fundal contractions.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Low-dose labour induction: Initial 1-2 milli units per minute, escalating by 1-2 milli units per minute every 15 to 20 minutes until adequate contractions occur.
High-dose labour induction: Initial 6-8 milli units per minute, escalating by 6-8 milli units per minute every 15 to 20 minutes until contractions are established.
Inevitable or missed miscarriage: 10-20 milli units per minute, up to a maximum dose of 30 units over 24 hours.
Active management of third stage of labour: 10 units IM or slow IV following delivery of the newborn.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical induction of labour in pre-eclampsia or gestational diabetes mellitus with a favourable cervix.
Augmentation of dysfunctional or protracted active labour.
Routine active management of the third stage of labour.
Prophylaxis and therapeutic arrest of uterine atony in postpartum haemorrhage (PPH).
Uterine contraction during caesarean section following delivery.
Evacuation assistance in inevitable or missed miscarriage and molar pregnancy.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Maternal: Nausea, vomiting, systemic hypotension following rapid bolus, uterine hypercontractility, uterine rupture, and maternal collapse.
Antidiuretic effect: Cross-reactivity with vasopressin receptors causes water intoxication, hyponatraemia, confusion, convulsions, coma, and congestive heart failure.
Fetal and neonatal: Fetal distress from uterine hyperstimulation, neonatal seizures, and hyperbilirubinaemia.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Absolute: Significant cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD), prior classical caesarean section or uterine rupture, transverse lie, cord prolapse, vasa praevia, and complete placenta praevia.
Obstetric hazards: Hyperactive or uncoordinated uterine contractility, and active genital herpes.
Caution required: Grand multiparity, multifetal gestation, polyhydramnios, maternal cardiac disease, and hypovolaemia.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Intramuscular route is strictly avoided for induction and augmentation of labour due to erratic absorption.
Plasma half-life is 3-5 minutes; clinical effects begin within 3-5 minutes and last up to 3 hours.
Uterine myometrium is relatively refractory to oxytocin in the first half of pregnancy due to low receptor density.
Can be stored at controlled room temperature below 30 degrees Celsius.
Syntometrine combines oxytocin 5 IU and ergometrine 0.5 mg.

viva.q: Why is rapid undiluted intravenous bolus injection of oxytocin hazardous?
viva.a: Rapid IV injection triggers precipitous systemic vasodilation, profound hypotension, reflex tachycardia, coronary hypoperfusion, and potential cardiovascular collapse.

viva.q: How does prolonged high-dose oxytocin infusion cause maternal water intoxication?
viva.a: Oxytocin shares structural homology with antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin); prolonged infusion with electrolyte-free fluids causes renal water retention and life-threatening hyponatraemia.

image.brief: Clear glass ampoule of synthetic oxytocin injection 10 IU/mL resting on a calibrated infusion calculation chart.

items.summary: An ergot alkaloid derivative producing sustained, tetanic myometrial contraction for the prevention and treatment of atonic postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Semi-synthetic ergot alkaloid derivative of ergometrine.
Marketed commercially under trade names Methergin and Utergin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral tablets for puerperal uterine involution.
Intramuscular injection (standard obstetric administration route).
Intravenous route is not routine and requires extreme caution.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Acts as a partial agonist at alpha-adrenergic, serotonergic, and dopaminergic receptors.
Induces sustained basal hypertonus and repetitive tetanic contractions in both upper and lower uterine segments.
Constricts peripheral vascular smooth muscle beds.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral puerperal therapy: 0.2 mg (200 micrograms) orally, 2-4 times daily for up to one week.
Intramuscular: 0.2 mg (200 micrograms) IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder in active management of third stage of labour.
Intravenous: Not administered routinely; if essential, give 0.2 mg very slowly over at least 1 minute with pulse and BP monitoring.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Active management of the third stage of labour when oxytocin is unavailable.
Prophylaxis against atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
Therapeutic control of established atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
Facilitation of uterine contraction at the time of placental separation.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Severe arterial hypertension, throbbing headache, and eclamptic seizures.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and severe uterine after-pains.
Severe coronary vasoconstriction, angina, myocardial infarction, bowel infarction, and peripheral digit gangrene.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and chronic gestational hypertension.
Organic maternal heart disease.
Multiple pregnancy before delivery of the final fetus.
Rhesus-negative isoimmunisation (risk of fetomaternal microtransfusion).
Never used for induction or augmentation of labour due to risk of tetanic rupture.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Routine intravenous push is contraindicated due to hazards of acute hypertensive stroke and coronary spasm.
Onset of action: oral takes 10 minutes, IM takes 7 minutes, and IV acts within 1 minute.
Acts uniformly on both upper and lower uterine segments, risking entrapment if given before delivery of the baby.
Syntometrine is a fixed combination of oxytocin 5 IU and ergometrine 0.5 mg.

viva.q: Why is methylergometrine contraindicated in women with pre-eclampsia or chronic hypertension?
viva.a: It causes intense generalized alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, which can precipitate malignant hypertension, acute heart failure, intracerebral haemorrhage, or convulsions.

viva.q: Why must methylergometrine never be administered before delivery of the baby?
viva.a: It triggers intense tetanic myometrial contractions without physiological relaxation, leading to acute fetal asphyxia and uterine rupture.

image.brief: Amber glass ampoule containing 0.2 mg/mL methylergometrine maleate solution beside a blister strip of 0.125 mg tablets on a white work tray.

items.summary: A synthetic 15-methyl analogue of prostaglandin F2-alpha used parenterally for refractory atonic postpartum haemorrhage and second-trimester pregnancy termination.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic 15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue resistant to enzymatic metabolic degradation.
Brand trade names include Prostodin, Hemabate, and Carboprost.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by deep intramuscular injection.
Can be administered by direct intramyometrial injection during caesarean section laparotomy.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Binds to prostanoid FP receptors on myometrial smooth muscle, augmenting membrane permeability and sensitising tissue to oxytocin.
Provokes intense, sustained uterine contractions and myometrial vasoconstriction to stem placental site bleeding.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Standard intramuscular dose: 0.25 mg (250 micrograms) deep IM.
May be repeated every 15 minutes as needed, up to a maximum of 8 doses (total cumulative dose 2 mg).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Second-line management of severe refractory atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
Prophylaxis against severe PPH in high-risk women.
Abortifacient for elective termination of pregnancy in the second trimester.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Secretory diarrhoea, severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping.
Pyrexia, chills, shivering, and systemic malaise.
Bronchospasm and ventilation-perfusion mismatch.
Systemic hypertension or transient hypotension.
Uterine hyperstimulation and cervical or uterine rupture.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active bronchial asthma due to intense bronchoconstrictor activity.
Severe cardiac or chronic pulmonary disease.
Previous caesarean section scar when used for mid-trimester abortion.
Incomplete abortion with open sepsis and acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: If uterine atony persists after the second of 8 potential doses, the patient must be transferred to the operating theatre anticipating laparotomy.
Direct intramyometrial injection may be given during caesarean laparotomy if conservative medical measures fail.
Must be refrigerated between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius to maintain chemical potency.

viva.q: Why is active bronchial asthma an absolute contraindication to carboprost administration?
viva.a: Prostaglandin F2-alpha stimulates bronchial smooth muscle FP receptors, triggering severe refractory bronchoconstriction and life-threatening respiratory arrest.

viva.q: How many doses of carboprost 0.25 mg may be given for atonic PPH, and what action is taken if bleeding continues after two doses?
viva.a: A maximum of 8 doses may be given at 15-minute intervals; if atony persists after the second dose, theatre transfer for laparotomy is prepared.

image.brief: One-millilitre glass ampoule containing 250 micrograms/mL carboprost tromethamine resting on a cold-pack storage container.

items.summary: An anticholinergic antimuscarinic smooth muscle relaxant used historically to hasten cervical dilatation during the first stage of labour.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Quaternary ammonium anticholinergic, antimuscarinic smooth muscle relaxant.
Proprietary formulations include Epidosin and Valamate.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral administration.
Intramuscular injection.
Intravenous injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively antagonises muscarinic cholinergic receptors, relaxing smooth muscle structures.
Overcomes cervical muscular spasm, accelerating cervical dilatation to shorten the duration of labour.
Relaxes visceral smooth muscle in the biliary tract, gastrointestinal tract, and urinary system.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral dose: 10-20 mg BD/TDS.
Parenteral dose: 4-8 mg administered via intramuscular or slow intravenous injection.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Facilitation of cervical dilatation in protracted first stage of labour.
Relief of gastrointestinal spasm and tenesmus.
Treatment of acute biliary colic.
Management of acute ureteric and urinary colic.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and cutaneous anhidrosis with dry skin.
Mydriasis (pupillary dilatation) and blurred near vision.
Sinus tachycardia and cardiac arrhythmias.
Urinary hesitancy and acute urinary retention.
Constipation, dysphagia, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and headache.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Narrow-angle glaucoma.
Severe cardiac disease, cardiac arrhythmias, and heart block.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and paralytic ileus.
Myasthenia gravis, toxic megacolon, and hyperthyroidism.
Porphyria and known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What is the claimed mechanism of valethamate bromide in shortening the duration of labour?
viva.a: It exerts an antimuscarinic spasmolytic action on the circular smooth muscle fibres of the cervix, promoting relaxation and faster cervical effacement and dilatation.

viva.q: List three classic anticholinergic side effects observed with parenteral valethamate bromide.
viva.a: Maternal sinus tachycardia, dry mouth (xerostomia), and pupillary dilatation (mydriasis) causing blurred near vision.

image.brief: Clear glass 1 mL ampoule of valethamate bromide 8 mg/mL injection beside a blister card of 10 mg sugar-coated tablets on a white clinic surface.

items.summary: A synthetic competitive progesterone receptor antagonist used in combination with misoprostol for medical termination of early pregnancy.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic 19-norsteroid acting as a competitive progesterone receptor antagonist.
Known scientifically as RU-486; commercial brands include Mifeprin, Mifegest, and Mifebort.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively blocks intracellular progesterone receptors in the presence of progesterone.
Causes decidual necrosis and breakdown, triggering detachment of the blastocyst.
Suppresses syncytiotrophoblast hCG production, inducing luteolysis and declining corpus luteum progesterone secretion.
Promotes cervical ripening, stimulates endogenous prostaglandin release, and sensitises myometrium to exogenous prostaglandins.
Exhibits antiglucocorticoid and weak antiandrogenic activity.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Medical termination of pregnancy: 200 mg single oral dose, followed after 24-48 hours by misoprostol.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical termination of early intrauterine pregnancy in conjunction with a prostaglandin analogue.
Off-label use as an emergency post-coital contraceptive.
Hyperglycaemia control in patients with Cushing syndrome and secondary type 2 diabetes mellitus.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Uterine abdominal cramping and pelvic pain.
Vaginal bleeding and spotting lasting an average of up to 3 weeks.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness, fatigue, and low-grade fever.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Suspected or confirmed ectopic pregnancy.
Retained intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) in situ.
Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency or adrenal failure.
Concurrent long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy.
Severe bleeding diatheses or concurrent anticoagulant therapy.

viva.q: Explain how mifepristone primes the uterus for misoprostol-induced medical abortion.
viva.a: It blocks progesterone receptors, causing decidual necrosis, blastocyst detachment, cervical softening, and up-regulation of myometrial prostaglandin receptors.

viva.q: Why is an intrauterine device (IUCD) a contraindication to medical termination of pregnancy with mifepristone?
viva.a: The device must be removed first because foreign bodies increase the risk of severe pelvic infection, sepsis, and mechanical uterine perforation during abortion.

image.brief: Individual blister packaging displaying a single light yellow 200 mg mifepristone tablet on a clean white consultation desk.

items.summary: A stable synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue widely used for medical abortion, labour induction, cervical priming, and postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) methyl ester analogue.
Trade brand preparations include Zitotec, Cytolog, Misoprost, and Cytotec.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral, sublingual, vaginal, and rectal administration routes.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Selectively binds to myometrial prostanoid EP receptors, augmenting intracellular calcium.
Promotes cervical connective tissue remodeling, effacement, and ripening.
Induces strong myometrial contractions leading to evacuation of intrauterine gestational tissue.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Dose ranges from 50 micrograms to 1000 micrograms depending on clinical indication.
Medical termination of pregnancy: Mifepristone 200 milligrams + 600 micrograms misoprostol.
Induction of labour: 25-50 micrograms vaginally or orally.
Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage: 400-1000 micrograms rectally, sublingually, or orally.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Induction of labour in intrauterine fetal demise (IUD).
Medical induction of first- and second-trimester abortion.
Medical evacuation of missed miscarriage.
Cervical priming prior to gynaecological procedures (hysteroscopy, IUCD or Mirena insertion, surgical evacuation).
Prophylaxis and treatment of atonic postpartum haemorrhage.
Treatment and prevention of gastric mucosal ulcers in non-pregnant adults.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Secretory diarrhoea, flatulence, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.
Transient pyrexia, shivering, chills, and headache.
Uterine tachysystole and hyperstimulation.
Uterine rupture, especially in women with prior scarred uteri.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Gastric ulcer treatment during pregnancy due to abortifacient and teratogenic risks.
Known prostaglandin hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: A critical drug for PPH prevention in low-resource settings because it is inexpensive, heat-stable without refrigeration, and easy to administer.

viva.q: Why is misoprostol particularly invaluable for managing postpartum haemorrhage in resource-limited settings?
viva.a: It is inexpensive, shelf-stable at room temperature without cold-chain storage, active via oral or rectal routes, and readily accessible.

viva.q: What route and dosage of misoprostol are recommended for labour induction in intrauterine fetal demise?
viva.a: 25 to 50 micrograms administered vaginally or orally every 4 to 6 hours, adjusted for gestational age and previous uterine scars.

image.brief: Blister strip displaying four hexagonal white 200 microgram misoprostol tablets on a clinical stainless steel tray.

items.summary: A folic acid antagonist antimetabolite used for medical management of unruptured ectopic pregnancy and gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Folic acid analogue antimetabolite and antineoplastic agent.
Trade names include Mexate and Trexall.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered via intramuscular, intravenous, oral, subcutaneous, and intrathecal routes.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).
Halts purine nucleotide and thymidylate biosynthesis, blocking DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis.
Selectively arrests cell replication during the synthetic S-phase of the mitotic cell cycle.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Ectopic pregnancy single-dose regimen: 50 mg/m2 body surface area IM.
Ectopic pregnancy multi-dose regimen: 1 mg/kg IM on days 1, 3, 5, 7 alternating with folinic acid rescue on days 2, 4, 6, 8.
Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN): Single-agent methotrexate for low-risk disease; combination chemotherapy regimens for high-risk disease.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical management of unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
Treatment of low-risk and high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
Systemic therapy for osteosarcoma, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, and head and neck neoplasms.
Immunosuppression in severe rheumatoid arthritis and refractory psoriasis.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Gastrointestinal: Glossitis, stomatitis, gingivitis, oral mucositis, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and abdominal pain.
Respiratory: Pharyngitis and pulmonary infiltrates.
Systemic: Bone marrow myelosuppression (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia), acute renal failure, hepatic necrosis, cutaneous photosensitivity, and alopecia.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Ectopic pregnancy displaying embryonic cardiac activity or beta-hCG over 5000 IU/L.
Pre-existing hepatic failure or severe renal failure.
Severe haematological cytopenias or blood dyscrasias.
Active viable intrauterine pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Ectopic pregnancy protocol: Serum hCG is assayed on days 4 and 7; if the decline is under 15%, a repeat dose is administered; if greater than 15%, follow up weekly.
High-risk GTN multi-agent regimen EMA-CO: Etoposide + Methotrexate + Actinomycin-D + Cyclophosphamide + Oncovin (vincristine).
Alternative high-risk GTN regimen EMA-EP: Etoposide + Methotrexate + Actinomycin-D + Etoposide + Cisplatin.

viva.q: Describe the monitoring criteria for success after single-dose methotrexate in ectopic pregnancy.
viva.a: Serum beta-hCG levels are measured on days 4 and 7; a decline of at least 15% between days 4 and 7 indicates therapeutic success.

viva.q: What drugs constitute the EMA-CO combination chemotherapy protocol in high-risk GTN?
viva.a: Etoposide, Methotrexate, Actinomycin-D, Cyclophosphamide, and Oncovin (vincristine).

image.brief: Amber glass 2 mL vial containing 50 mg/2 mL methotrexate injection next to a cytotoxic hazard warning disposal box.

items.summary: Essential oral and parenteral iron preparations used for prophylaxis and curative treatment of maternal iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Oral and parenteral elemental iron replacement formulations.
Oral salts: Ferrous sulphate (65 mg elemental iron in 325 mg tablet), ferrous fumarate (65 mg elemental iron in 325 mg tablet), and ferrous gluconate (34 mg elemental iron in 300 mg tablet).
Intramuscular: Iron dextran (Imferon, 50 mg/mL elemental iron) and iron sorbitol citrate (Jectofer).
Intravenous: Ferric gluconate (12.5 mg/mL), iron sucrose (20 mg/mL), and ferric carboxymaltose (up to 1000 mg single dose).

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral ingestion.
Deep intramuscular injection using the Z-track technique.
Intravenous infusion.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Prophylactic oral dose: 100 mg elemental iron per day.
Curative oral dose: 3 tablets daily until haemoglobin normalises, then 1 tablet daily for 100 days.
Parenteral IM dose: 50 mg/mL IM for 10 days; calculation: 0.3 x W x (100 - Hb%) mg + 50% (where W is body weight in pounds).

Intravenous iron sucrose: 100 mg diluted in 100 mL normal saline infused over 15 minutes, 2-3 times weekly; calculation: (2.3 x W x D) + 500 mg (where W is weight in kg, D is target Hb minus actual Hb in g/dL).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prophylaxis and correction of nutritional iron-deficiency anaemia during pregnancy and lactation.
Parenteral restoration of iron reserves in non-compliant patients or those presenting near term.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Oral disadvantages: Epigastric distress, nausea, vomiting, constipation or dark diarrhoea, and poor intestinal absorption.
Intramuscular disadvantages: Intense injection pain, sterile gluteal abscess, persistent skin hyperpigmentation, and systemic hypersensitivity.
Intravenous disadvantages: Phlebitis, transient hypotension, anaphylactoid reactions, and skin tattooing upon extravasation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Haemoglobin response: Oral and IM increase haemoglobin by 0.3-1 g/week; IV increases haemoglobin by approximately 1 g/week.
Erythropoietin (50-150 units/kg SC 2-3 times/week) raises haemoglobin by 2 g/week; one unit of transfused packed red blood cells raises haemoglobin by 1 g/dL.
Oral iron should be stopped at least 24 hours before parenteral iron therapy, and restarted 4-5 days after completing IV treatment.
Oral supplementation is routinely initiated in the second trimester to avoid aggravating first-trimester morning sickness.
Ferric carboxymaltose provides the distinct advantage of delivering up to 1000 mg elemental iron in a single rapid infusion.

viva.q: State Ganzoni's formula for calculating the total parenteral intravenous iron requirement.
viva.a: Total iron deficit in mg equals [Body weight in kg x (Target Hb minus Actual Hb in g/dL) x 2.4] plus 500 mg for iron depot stores.

viva.q: Why is oral iron therapy routinely deferred until after the first trimester of pregnancy?
