viva.a: Iron requirements in early gestation are minimal, and oral iron causes gastric irritation that worsens first-trimester nausea and hyperemesis gravidarum.

image.brief: Clear glass 5 mL ampoule of iron sucrose (100 mg/5 mL) beside a 100 mL normal saline infusion bottle and blister pack of ferrous sulphate tablets.

items.summary: A water-soluble B-complex vitamin essential for one-carbon transfers, DNA synthesis, and prevention of fetal neural tube defects.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Water-soluble synthetic form of vitamin B9 (folate).
Trade formulations include Fol B, Folvite, and Neofol.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Daily requirement: Non-pregnant women need 50-100 micrograms/day; pregnant women need 400 micrograms/day (WHO recommends 800 micrograms/day in pregnancy, 600 micrograms/day in lactation).
Prophylactic dose: 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) per day, taken 3 months before conception and continuing through the first 3 months of pregnancy.
Therapeutic dose: 5 mg per day for 4-6 weeks for established deficiency or high-risk pregnancies.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Primary prevention of neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida, encephalocele).
Treatment of maternal megaloblastic anaemia secondary to folate deficiency.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Gastrointestinal upset including nausea, anorexia, and abdominal fullness.
Altered or bitter taste sensation in the mouth.
Peripheral numbness and tingling sensation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: High-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) is indicated if the previous child had a neural tube defect, in maternal diabetes, on anticonvulsant therapy, or with inflammatory bowel disease.
Folic acid food fortification in flour is established in several nations including the UK and USA.
Response to therapy: Fall in serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) by 4-5 days, accompanied by reticulocytosis within 5-8 days.
Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia; treated with 1 mg IM on alternate days for 2 weeks, then 1 mg IM monthly for 6 months.

viva.q: What is the recommended periconceptional dose of folic acid for a woman who previously had a baby with spina bifida?
viva.a: 5 mg daily, initiated at least one to three months prior to conception and continued throughout the first trimester.

viva.q: Which clinical laboratory changes confirm a positive haematological response to folic acid therapy in megaloblastic anaemia?
viva.a: A rapid fall in serum lactate dehydrogenase within 4 to 5 days followed by a distinct reticulocyte peak between days 5 and 8.

image.brief: Blister strip of small circular 5 mg yellow folic acid tablets beside a 400 microgram prenatal tablet bottle on a white surface.

items.summary: An essential dietary mineral supplemented during pregnancy and lactation to support fetal skeletal ossification and lower pre-eclampsia risk.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Essential macronutrient and mineral electrolyte supplement.
Commercial preparations include Calcimax, Acucal, and Shelcal.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Recommended dietary intake: 800 mg/day in adults, 1000 mg/day in pregnancy, and 1300 mg/day during lactation.
Supplemental dosage: 500 mg BD dose or 1 gm OD taken with meals.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Replenishes maternal skeletal calcium stores and provides fetal calcium transfer, particularly in the third trimester.
Supports fetal skeletal growth and tooth development.
Facilitates normal neuromuscular transmission and physiological coagulation cascade activity.
Administered to women at high risk of pre-eclampsia to lower the incidence of hypertensive disorders.
Reduces neonatal rickets and the incidence of low birth weight.
Prevents postmenopausal osteoporosis in gynaecological practice.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Predisposition to urinary tract infections.
Formation of nephrolithiasis and renal calculi.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Dietary oxalates, phosphates, and phytates significantly reduce intestinal calcium bioavailability.
Total serum calcium falls physiologically during pregnancy due to dilution, necessitating dietary supplementation.

viva.q: Why is routine calcium supplementation recommended by the WHO for pre-eclampsia prevention?
viva.a: In populations with low baseline dietary calcium, supplementing 1.5 to 2.0 g elemental calcium daily significantly reduces the risk of gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia.

viva.q: What dietary factors impair the intestinal absorption of oral calcium supplements?
viva.a: Dietary phytates (unrefined cereals), oxalates (spinach, tea), and high phosphates bind calcium in the gut lumen, forming insoluble unabsorbed complexes.

image.brief: Blister strip containing 500 mg calcium carbonate with vitamin D3 tablets beside an open packaging box on a consultation desk.

items.summary: A synthetic lysine analogue antifibrinolytic used for heavy menstrual bleeding, surgical haemostasis, and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic lysine derivative and competitive antifibrinolytic agent.
Proprietary market brands include Pause, Trapic, T Stat, Tranexa, and Xamic.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral administration.
Intravenous bolus injection or infusion.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively blocks lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its activation into fibrin-degrading plasmin.
Directly inhibits plasmin enzymatic activity at higher therapeutic concentrations, stabilising fibrin hemostatic plugs.
Shares a similar pharmacological mechanism with aminocaproic acid.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral: 2-4 gm per day in divided doses.
IV: 1-3 gm per day in divided doses (commonly 1 gm slow IV over 10 minutes in acute haemorrhage).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical management of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and ovulatory menorrhagia.
Haemostatic reduction of blood loss in obstetric haemorrhage and traumatic bleeding.
Minimising blood loss following gynaecological and pelvic surgery.
Control of severe epistaxis.
Dental extraction prophylaxis in patients with haemophilia without replacement therapy.
Long-term prophylaxis in hereditary angioedema.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea.
Systemic: Transient hypotension on rapid IV injection, visual disturbances, dizziness, headache, fatigue, and allergic anaphylaxis.
Thromboembolic risks: Venous thromboembolism (rare), pulmonary embolism, cerebral stroke, and myocardial infarction.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism).
Known drug hypersensitivity.
History of thromboembolic disease.

viva.q: What is the biochemical mechanism by which tranexamic acid inhibits fibrinolysis?
viva.a: It reversibly occupies the lysine-binding domains of plasminogen, preventing plasminogen from binding to fibrin and converting into active plasmin.

viva.q: What did the WOMAN trial demonstrate regarding tranexamic acid in postpartum haemorrhage?
viva.a: Administering 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth significantly reduces maternal mortality due to bleeding without increasing the risk of thromboembolic events.

image.brief: Clear glass 5 mL ampoule of tranexamic acid 100 mg/mL (500 mg total) beside a blister pack of 500 mg oral tablets on a clean neutral background.

items.summary: Synthetic decapeptide GnRH analogues that cause pituitary receptor down-regulation, inducing medical hypogonadism for endometriosis and assisted reproduction.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic peptide analogues of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
Representative trade preparations include Lupride (leuprolide), Busarlin (buserelin), and Nasarel nasal spray (nafarelin).

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Intramuscular depot injection.
Subcutaneous injection.
Intranasal spray formulation.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Initially stimulates pituitary GnRH receptors, triggering a transient release flare of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH).
Continuous stimulation down-regulates and internalises GnRH receptors, suppressing gonadotropin secretion within 2-3 weeks.
Induces profound hypoestrogenism (pseudomenopause), causing atrophy of estrogen-dependent ectopic endometrial and leiomyomatous tissue.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Leuprolide acetate depot: 3.75 mg intramuscularly once every 4 weeks.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Induction of ovulation when clomiphene citrate and laparoscopic ovarian drilling fail.
Diagnostic evaluation of hypothalamic versus pituitary causes of primary amenorrhoea.
Adjunctive therapy in primary amenorrhoea management.
Pubertal suppression in constitutional precocious puberty.
Suppression of premature endogenous LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation in in vitro fertilisation (IVF).
Medical management of severe premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
Symptomatic shrinkage of uterine leiomyomas, endometriosis, and abnormal uterine bleeding.
Suppression of severe refractory hirsutism.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Hypoestrogenic state (pseudomenopause): Hot flushes, drenching night sweats, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and reduced libido.
Accelerated trabecular bone mineral density loss and osteoporosis.
Affective mood swings, depression, and headache.
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and multifetal gestation when used for ovulation induction.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding.
Premature ovarian failure.
Functional pituitary tumours.
Overt untreated thyroid dysfunction.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: When prescribed for longer than 6 months, add-back hormone replacement therapy (such as Tibolone) is mandatory to prevent osteoporosis and pathological fractures.
Leuprolide standard clinical dosage is 3.75 mg intramuscular depot.

viva.q: Why is add-back therapy mandatory when GnRH agonists are prescribed beyond 6 months?
viva.a: Profound prolonged hypoestrogenism causes rapid trabecular bone demineralisation; add-back low-dose estrogen-progestogen or tibolone preserves bone mass without reactivating disease.

viva.q: Explain the difference between the initial flare and therapeutic phase of GnRH agonists.
viva.a: Initial receptor activation causes a 1-2 week flare of FSH and LH; continuous exposure then down-regulates and desensitises pituitary receptors, achieving medical castration.

image.brief: Dual-chamber pre-filled depot syringe containing leuprolide acetate 3.75 mg lyophilised powder and diluent on an endocrinology clinic desk.

items.summary: A synthetic ethinyl testosterone derivative with androgenic and antigonadotropic properties, used for endometriosis, fibrocystic breast disease, and fibroids.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic derivative of 17-alpha-ethinyl testosterone.
Exhibits weak androgenic, weak progestogenic, anti-estrogenic, antigonadotropic, and anabolic properties.
Commercial formulations include Gynazol, Endozol, and Endometryl.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Suppresses the mid-cycle surge of LH and FSH by acting on the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian axis, lowering circulating estrogens.
Directly inhibits multiple steroidogenic enzymes in ovaries and adrenals, suppressing synthesis of estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.
Displaces testosterone from sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and reduces SHBG synthesis, elevating free circulating androgen levels.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Endometriosis: 200-400 mg OD/BD orally.
Fibrocystic breast disease: 100-400 mg OD/BD orally.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Symptomatic management of pelvic endometriosis.
Medical treatment of menorrhagia in abnormal uterine bleeding.
Pre-operative shrinkage of uterine leiomyomas.
Relief of severe premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
Treatment of fibrocystic disease of the breast.
Alleviation of severe cyclical and non-cyclical mastalgia (breast pain and tenderness).

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Androgenic: Hirsutism, oily skin, inflammatory acne, weight gain, and irreversible deepening of voice.
Hypoestrogenic: Hot flushes, night sweats, emotional lability, reduced libido, and atrophic vaginitis.
Metabolic and systemic: Breast atrophy, atherogenic lipid profile derangement, hepatotoxicity, nausea, vomiting, arthralgia, and muscle spasms.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pregnancy due to potent virilisation of the external genitalia in female fetuses.
Lactation.
Active hepatic diseases or hepatic impairment.
Severe renal disease or congestive cardiac failure.
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: Why is voice deepening considered a particularly critical adverse effect of danazol?
viva.a: Deepening of the voice is caused by structural androgen-mediated hypertrophy of vocal cord tissues and is typically permanent and irreversible despite drug cessation.

viva.q: What dangerous fetal malformation occurs if danazol is inadvertently taken during early pregnancy?
viva.a: Virilisation of the female fetus, manifesting as clitoromegaly, labial fusion, and pseudohermaphroditism.

image.brief: Blister packaging showing 100 mg and 200 mg white danazol capsules resting next to an instructional leaflet on a medical consultation table.

items.summary: A synthetic 19-nortestosterone steroid derivative with multi-modal actions used for medical treatment of endometriosis and fibroids.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic steroid derivative of 19-norethisterone possessing multi-modal endocrine actions.
Commercially prepared under trade names Dimetriose and Dimetrose.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by the oral route.
Vaginal administration.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Exerts central antigonadotropic actions to suppress pulsatile release of FSH and LH.
Inhibits ovarian steroidogenesis and increases sex hormone-binding globulin, elevating free testosterone.
Acts as a selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM) with mixed agonist and antagonist effects.
Exhibits mild androgenic and anabolic steroid properties, inducing cellular regression of endometriotic deposits.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Standard clinical regimen: 2.5-5 mg orally twice a week.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Medical treatment of pelvic endometriosis.
Management of menorrhagia associated with abnormal uterine bleeding.
Pre-operative medical management of uterine fibroids.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Cutaneous: Acne, seborrhoea with oily skin, and alopecia.
Endocrine and androgenic: Therapeutic amenorrhoea, fluid retention, weight gain, hirsutism, and voice deepening.
Teratogenic: Virilisation of the external genitalia in female fetuses.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pregnancy (causes female fetal virilisation).
Lactation.
Severe hepatic failure or active liver disease.
Renal failure.
Severe cardiac insufficiency.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What is the typical dosage schedule of gestrinone in pelvic endometriosis?
viva.a: 2.5 mg administered orally twice weekly, usually initiated on day 1 and day 4 of the menstrual cycle.

viva.q: How does gestrinone cause regression of endometriotic implants?
viva.a: By combined pituitary gonadotropin suppression and direct progesterone receptor modulation, creating an anovulatory, hypoestrogenic, and hyperandrogenic milieu that atrophies endometrium.

image.brief: Card pack containing four 2.5 mg gestrinone capsules with weekly day markings on a clean clinic surface.

items.summary: A synthetic valerate ester of natural 17-beta estradiol used for menopausal hormone replacement therapy, premature ovarian insufficiency, and IVF preparation.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic ester of naturally occurring bio-identical 17-beta estradiol.
Well-known pharmaceutical brands include Progynova and Evatone.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Cleaved in vivo to liberate natural 17-beta estradiol, supplementing declining endogenous estrogen levels during menopause.
Binds to nuclear estrogen receptors (ER-alpha and ER-beta), regulating transcription of estrogen-responsive target genes.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Hormone replacement: 1 mg-2 mg daily by mouth.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Estrogen-alone hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in hysterectomised women with vasomotor menopausal symptoms.
Combined HRT with a progestogen in women with an intact uterus to relieve menopausal symptoms without endometrial hyperplasia.
Physiological estrogen replacement in younger women diagnosed with premature ovarian failure.
Prevention of accelerated postmenopausal bone mineral density loss and osteoporosis.
Endometrial preparation and thickness maintenance during frozen embryo transfer cycles in IVF.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, bloating sensation, and flatulence.
Gynaecological/cutaneous: Vaginal candidiasis, generalized fluid retention, leg cramps, chloasma, and breast tenderness.
Vascular and hepatobiliary: Hypertension, venous thromboembolism (VTE), cholestatic jaundice, pancreatitis, and gall bladder disease.
Central: Dizziness, vascular headache, and exacerbation of migraine.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known or suspected breast carcinoma.
Estrogen-dependent endometrial carcinoma.
Primary hepatocellular carcinoma or active acute liver disease.
Active venous thromboembolism (VTE) or known hereditary thrombophilia.
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Recent stroke or acute myocardial infarction.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding.

viva.q: Why must estradiol valerate always be combined with a progestogen in women with an intact uterus?
viva.a: Unopposed estrogen stimulation provokes continuous endometrial glandular proliferation, leading to atypical endometrial hyperplasia and an elevated risk of endometrial adenocarcinoma.

viva.q: Name two major absolute cardiovascular contraindications to systemic estrogen replacement therapy.
viva.a: Active or previous venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) and recent arterial thromboembolic disease including ischaemic stroke or myocardial infarction.

image.brief: Circular calendar dial blister pack of 1 mg sugar-coated estradiol valerate tablets displayed flat on a clean white desk.

items.summary: A complex mixture of natural equine estrogen sulfates used for menopausal hormone replacement therapy, postmenopausal osteoporosis, and atrophic vaginitis.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Conjugated equine estrogen blend derived from pregnant mares urine.
Contains water-soluble sodium sulfate esters of estrone, equilin, and 17-alpha-estradiol.
Marketed globally under the proprietary brand Premarin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.
Administered intravenously for acute haemostatic control.
Topical intravaginal cream formulation.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: General therapeutic range: 0.3 mg-1.25 mg daily.
Postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms: Initial starting dose is 0.3 mg per day.
Postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention: Initial starting dose is 0.625 mg per day.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in hysterectomised women.
Combined HRT with a progestogen in women with an intact uterus suffering from menopausal symptoms.
Prevention of accelerated postmenopausal bone mineral density loss and osteoporosis.
Adjunctive therapy in select cases of advanced breast carcinoma.
Topical vaginal cream to alleviate postmenopausal atrophic vaginitis, vaginal dryness, itching, and dyspareunia.
Emergency medical haemostasis in acute severe abnormal uterine bleeding.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Vulvovaginal candidiasis and breakthrough vaginal spotting or bleeding.
Nocturnal leg cramps and pelvic dysmenorrhoea.
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and bloating.
Decreased sexual libido, dizziness, and headache.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known or suspected breast carcinoma.
Estrogen-dependent endometrial carcinoma and untreated endometrial hyperplasia.
Active hepatocellular carcinoma or acute liver disease.
Active venous thromboembolism (VTE) or documented thrombophilia.
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Recent ischaemic stroke or acute myocardial infarction.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What is the primary biological source of conjugated equine estrogens?
viva.a: It is purified from the concentrated urine of pregnant mares, consisting predominantly of estrone sulfate and equilin sulfate conjugates.

viva.q: What is the specific clinical role of topical conjugated estrogen vaginal cream in postmenopausal women?
viva.a: It treats local genitourinary syndrome of menopause, restoring vaginal rugae and moisture to alleviate atrophic vaginitis, pruritus, and dyspareunia.

image.brief: Blister card of maroon 0.625 mg oval coated conjugated estrogen tablets beside a tube of topical vaginal cream with an applicator on a clinic tray.

items.summary: Natural and synthetic progestational steroids used for luteal phase support, prevention of recurrent miscarriage, preterm labour prophylaxis, and AUB.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Natural and synthetic progestational steroidal hormones.
Dydrogesterone: Orally active retro-progesterone (Duphaston, Femoston).
Hydroxyprogesterone caproate: Long-acting synthetic depot ester (Proluton depot, Luteum depot, Maintane depot).
Micronised natural progesterone: Bio-identical progesterone (Susten, Cyclogest, Gestone).

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Dydrogesterone: Administered orally.
Hydroxyprogesterone caproate: Administered via deep intramuscular injection.
Natural progesterone: Formulated as oral capsules, vaginal pessaries, vaginal sustained-release gels, and intramuscular injections.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Dydrogesterone: Selective progestogenic actions without inhibiting ovulation; promotes secretory transformation and stable shedding of the endometrium.
Synthetic and natural progestogens: Suppress myometrial contractility, induce decidualisation, and support early gestational maintenance.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Dydrogesterone in miscarriage: 40 mg loading dose orally, then 10 mg BD/TDS until symptoms resolve.
Hydroxyprogesterone caproate for preterm birth prevention: 500 mg IM weekly, initiated from 16 weeks up to 37 weeks gestation.
Micronised progesterone: 100-200 mg OD/BD up to 16 weeks for sustaining early pregnancy; injection given usually from cycle day 15 onwards.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Management of threatened miscarriage and recurrent pregnancy loss.
Luteal phase support in assisted reproductive technology (IVF) and luteal phase deficiency.
Prophylaxis of recurrent preterm labour in women with prior spontaneous preterm birth.
Medical treatment of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) and secondary amenorrhoea.
Relief of premenstrual syndrome (PMS), severe dysmenorrhoea, and endometriosis.
Endometrial protection in combined hormone replacement therapy (HRT).
Adjunctive feminisation therapy in male-to-female transgender individuals.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Common: Mastalgia, breast tenderness, fluid retention, bloating sensation, weight gain, nausea, headache, and menstrual cycle irregularities.
Parenteral: Injection site induration, local pain, cutaneous bruising, pruritus, and sterile abscess formation.
Systemic: Insomnia, alopecia, drowsiness, and depression.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA, Meprate) 5-10 mg is used for progesterone withdrawal bleeding, secondary amenorrhoea, AUB, and endometrial hyperplasia.
High-dose medroxyprogesterone acetate is employed as palliative endocrine therapy in advanced recurrent endometrial adenocarcinoma.

viva.q: What is the evidence-based dose and timing of hydroxyprogesterone caproate for preventing preterm birth?
viva.a: 500 mg administered intramuscularly once weekly, initiated between 16 and 20 weeks gestation and continued until 36 to 37 weeks.

viva.q: Why does dydrogesterone not impede conception when prescribed for luteal phase deficiency?
viva.a: Dydrogesterone is a selective retro-progesterone that transforms the endometrium into a receptive secretory state without suppressing hypothalamic-pituitary ovulation.

image.brief: Blister strip of 10 mg film-coated dydrogesterone tablets beside an ampoule of 500 mg/2 mL hydroxyprogesterone caproate on a consultation desk.

items.summary: A placental glycoprotein hormone with luteinising hormone activity, used to trigger final oocyte maturation, induce ovulation, and support early pregnancy.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Naturally occurring heterodimeric placental glycoprotein hormone.
Composed of an alpha subunit (homologous to LH, FSH, and TSH) and a unique beta subunit.
Commercial preparations include Pregnyl, HUCOG, and Ferticog.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by subcutaneous injection.
Administered via deep intramuscular injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Binds directly to luteinising hormone/choriogonadotropin (LH/CG) transmembrane receptors on ovarian granulosacells.
Mimics the mid-cycle endogenous LH surge, triggering final oocyte meiosis and inducing follicular rupture 32 to 36 hours post-injection.
Stimulates ovarian corpus luteum maintenance and sustained progesterone secretion during early gestation.
Promotes testicular Leydig cell testosterone secretion in males.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Ovulation induction trigger: 5000-10000 IU administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly once a mature lead follicle reaches 18-20 mm.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Triggering ovulation in anovulatory infertility following follicle maturation.
Induction of final oocyte maturation prior to transvaginal oocyte retrieval in IVF.
Enhancement of spermatogenesis and sperm density in oligospermic males.
Stimulation of pubertal development in adolescent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Treatment of prepubertal cryptorchidism (undescended testes).
Luteal phase support in recurrent pregnancy loss and corpus luteum insufficiency.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and multifetal gestation.
Local injection site reactions: erythema, swelling, tenderness, and pain.
Cutaneous urticarial rash and low-grade pyrexia.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Unexplained or undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Estrogen-dependent neoplasms: breast, uterine, or ovarian carcinoma.
Pre-existing ovarian cysts or non-polycystic ovarian enlargement.
Known hypersensitivity to gonadotropin preparations.

viva.q: What is the expected time interval between an hCG trigger injection and follicular ovulation?
viva.a: Ovulation occurs consistently between 32 and 36 hours following intramuscular or subcutaneous hCG administration.

viva.q: What serious iatrogenic complication must be anticipated when using hCG to trigger ovulation in superovulated ovaries?
viva.a: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), driven by vascular endothelial growth factor release causing marked third-space fluid shifts.

image.brief: Lyophilised vial of 5000 IU human chorionic gonadotropin powder beside a 1 mL sterile water diluent ampoule on a medical tray.

items.summary: A purified urinary gonadotropin preparation containing equal bioactivity of FSH and LH, used for controlled ovarian stimulation and anovulatory infertility.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Natural gonadotropin preparation biologically extracted from the postmenopausal urine of women.
Standard preparations provide 75 IU LH + 75 IU FSH or 150 IU LH + 150 IU FSH per vial.
Proprietary brands include Pergonal, Menopur, Menogon, Humegon, and HUMOG.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by intramuscular injection.
Administered via subcutaneous injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Exogenous FSH binds to follicular granulosa cell receptors, stimulating recruitment and growth of ovarian follicles.
Exogenous LH binds to theca cell receptors, promoting androgen substrate production for aromatisation into estradiol.
Generates mature pre-ovulatory Graafian follicles in anovulatory infertile women.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Anovulatory infertility regimen: Generally 75 IU is given for 7 days, monitored with serial transvaginal ultrasound; increments of 37.5 IU weekly may be added to a maximum of 225 IU.
The starting daily dose is up to a maximum of 150 IU.
Dosing is strictly individualised prior to assisted reproductive technology (ART) cycles.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Second-line ovulation induction when clomiphene citrate therapy fails to achieve ovulation.
Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation for multiple follicle recruitment in IVF and GIFT cycles.
Stimulation of spermatogenesis in hypogonadotropic hypogonadal men.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
Multiple gestations (predominantly twins and higher-order multifetal pregnancies).
Elevated incidence of early miscarriage compared with spontaneous conceptions.
Ectopic pregnancy in women with pre-existing tubal pathology.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Primary hypergonadotropic ovarian failure (elevated baseline gonadotropins).
Primary testicular failure in males.
Pituitary or hypothalamic intracranial tumours.
Estrogen-dependent tumours (uterine, breast, or ovarian carcinoma).
Undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding.
Active pregnancy and known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Highly purified and recombinant gonadotropins avoid foreign urinary protein impurities and eliminate batch-to-batch potency variation.

viva.q: What hormonal constituents and bioactivities are present in standard human menopausal gonadotropin (menotropin)?
viva.a: Each standard vial provides an equal biological ratio of 75 IU follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and 75 IU luteinising hormone (LH).

viva.q: How is ovarian response monitored during an hMG ovulation induction cycle to avert OHSS?
viva.a: Serial transvaginal ultrasonography to measure follicular diameters and number, combined with serum estradiol level tracking.

image.brief: Glass vial of lyophilised menotropin (75 IU FSH + 75 IU LH) powder with diluent ampoule and a 1 mL subcutaneous injection syringe on a clinic desk.

items.summary: An orally active selective estrogen receptor modulator used as first-line therapy for ovulation induction in normogonadotropic anovulatory infertility.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Non-steroidal triphenylethylene selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).
Marketed commercially under trade names Fertomid, Siphene, and Ovipreg.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Binds competitively to hypothalamic and pituitary estrogen receptors, depleting them for an extended duration.
Blocks endogenous negative feedback inhibition of circulating estrogens at the hypothalamus.
Stimulates pulsatile release of GnRH, amplifying pituitary FSH and LH secretion to drive follicular recruitment.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Initial starting dose: 50 mg daily taken on cycle days 1-5 (or days 2-6 / 3-7).
If anovulation persists, the dose may be escalated in subsequent cycles to 100 mg and up to a maximum of 150 mg daily.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: First-line ovulation induction in World Health Organization Group II anovulatory infertility (polycystic ovary syndrome).
Treatment of luteal phase defect secondary to ovulatory dysfunction.
Off-label empirical treatment of idiopathic male oligospermia.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Vasomotor hot flushes, night sweats, and facial warmth.
Nausea, vomiting, and pelvic abdominal distension.
Bilateral ovarian enlargement and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).
Scintillating scotomas, visual blurring, and photophobia.
Breast tenderness and throbbing headache.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active pregnancy.
Chronic hepatic disease or liver dysfunction.
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Uncontrolled thyroid or adrenal endocrinopathies.
Suspected pituitary tumours.
Endometrial carcinoma.
Pre-existing ovarian cysts or pelvic masses unrelated to polycystic ovaries.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Ovulation occurs in approximately 70-80% of treated responders.
Cumulative pregnancy conception rate reaches 60-70% over 6 ovulatory treatment cycles.
Multifetal pregnancy rate is roughly 10-11%, predominantly dichorionic diamniotic twins.
Other important SERMs include Tamoxifen (breast cancer), Raloxifene (osteoporosis and breast cancer), and Ormeloxifene (contraception and AUB).
Clomiphene resistance denotes failure to achieve ovulation at 150 mg daily; clomiphene failure denotes failure to conceive despite ovulatory cycles.

viva.q: What is the biological mechanism of clomifene citrate in inducing follicular ovulation?
viva.a: It antagonises hypothalamic estrogen receptors, abolishing negative feedback to provoke an increase in pulsatile GnRH and pituitary FSH secretion.

viva.q: Differentiate between clomifene resistance and clomifene failure.
viva.a: Clomifene resistance means inability to achieve ovulation despite maximum daily doses of 150 mg; clomifene failure means successful ovulation without achieving pregnancy.

image.brief: Blister strip containing five small circular white 50 mg clomifene citrate tablets on a medical consultation desk.

items.summary: A first-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator used for estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer, mastalgia, and reserve ovulation induction.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: First-generation synthetic triphenylethylene selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).
Marketed worldwide under the brand name Nolvadex.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Exerts competitive estrogen receptor antagonist activity on mammary breast tissue.
Acts as a partial estrogen receptor agonist on the uterine endometrium, promoting glandular proliferation.
Acts as an estrogen agonist on trabecular and cortical bone, conserving bone mineral density.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Carcinoma breast therapy: 20 mg BD orally (or 20 mg once daily for 5-10 years).
Cyclical and non-cyclical mastalgia: 10 mg OD orally.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Adjuvant endocrine therapy for estrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma in pre- and post-menopausal women.
Chemoprevention against invasive breast cancer following surgery or radiotherapy in high-risk women.
Prevention of accelerated postmenopausal bone mineral density loss.
Medical treatment of severe refractory mastalgia.
Alternative second-line agent for ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Vasomotor hot flushes, night sweats, nausea, and vomiting.
Menstrual irregularities, secondary amenorrhoea, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Endometrial hyperplasia, benign endometrial polyps, and elevated risk of endometrial adenocarcinoma.
Alopecia, cutaneous rashes, mental depression, peripheral oedema, and thromboembolism.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active or prior venous thromboembolism (VTE).
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Active pregnancy.
Documented endometrial carcinoma or severe atypical endometrial hyperplasia.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Reduces circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels.
Preserves and improves postmenopausal bone mineral mass.
Ovulation and pregnancy success rates are comparable to clomifene citrate when used for ovulation induction.

viva.q: Why does long-term tamoxifen therapy warrant regular gynaecological surveillance?
viva.a: Its partial agonistic activity on the endometrium stimulates glandular proliferation, increasing the incidence of endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, and endometrial carcinoma.

viva.q: Describe the tissue-specific agonistic and antagonistic spectrum of tamoxifen.
viva.a: It acts as an antagonist on mammary breast tissue, but behaves as an agonist on the uterine endometrium, bone mineral density, and circulating lipid profiles.

image.brief: Blister strip of circular white 20 mg tamoxifen citrate tablets displayed flat on a clean clinical work surface.

items.summary: A second-generation selective estrogen receptor modulator used for postmenopausal osteoporosis and breast cancer prevention, without endometrial stimulation.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Second-generation synthetic benzothiophene selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).
Formulated under the international brand name Evista.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in bone tissue, inhibiting osteoclastic resorption and preserving trabecular bone.
Acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in mammary breast tissue.
Acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist on uterine endometrial tissue, causing no endometrial hypertrophy or bleeding.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention and treatment: 60 mg per day orally taken with or without food.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Prevention of postmenopausal bone loss and osteoporosis.
Treatment of established postmenopausal osteoporosis.
Significant reduction in the incidence of new vertebral compression fractures.
Reduction in the long-term risk of invasive estrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Vasomotor hot flushes and nocturnal sweating.
Nocturnal leg cramps and peripheral muscular spasms.
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pulmonary embolism.
Nausea, cutaneous rashes, insomnia, bronchitis, pharyngitis, and gastroenteritis.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Active or past history of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism).
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Pregnancy and lactation.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: How does the endometrial profile of raloxifene differ fundamentally from tamoxifen?
viva.a: Raloxifene acts as a complete antagonist on the endometrium, avoiding the endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, and endometrial cancer risks linked to tamoxifen.

viva.q: What is the primary clinical indication and major life-threatening risk of raloxifene?
viva.a: Indicated for postmenopausal osteoporosis and breast cancer chemoprevention; its major life-threatening adverse effect is a three-fold increase in venous thromboembolism.

image.brief: Blister packaging showing oval white 60 mg film-coated raloxifene tablets alongside a bone density DXA scan report on a desk.

items.summary: A non-hormonal, non-steroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator used in India as a weekly oral contraceptive and for abnormal uterine bleeding.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Third-generation non-steroidal, non-hormonal selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM).
Originated and developed in India; marketed under trade names Saheli, Sevista, and Novex DS.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Exerts potent anti-estrogenic antagonist activity on the uterine endometrium and breast tissue.
Maintains weak estrogen agonistic activity on skeletal bone.
Accelerates blastocyst transit through the Fallopian tube and desynchronises endometrial receptivity, preventing blastocyst implantation.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: As an oral contraceptive: 30 mg twice weekly for the first 12 weeks, followed by 30 mg once weekly from the 13th week onwards.
In abnormal uterine bleeding: 60 mg twice a week for the first 12 weeks, then 60 mg once a week for the next 12 weeks, and 30 mg once a week from the 13th week onwards.
First dose is ingested on the first day of menstrual bleeding, and subsequent doses follow the scheduled fixed days irrespective of bleeding.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Non-hormonal oral spacing contraception.
Medical treatment of menorrhagia in abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB).
Adjunctive therapy in estrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma.
Symptomatic management of severe mastalgia and benign fibroadenoma.
Relief of premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
Preservation of postmenopausal bone mass.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Menstrual cycle prolongation, oligomenorrhoea, and therapeutic amenorrhoea.
Nausea, vomiting, headache, and mild weight gain.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) due to propensity to induce follicular cysts.
Active hepatic dysfunction or severe liver disease.
Severe chronic renal disease.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: Outline the dosing protocol for ormeloxifene (Centchroman) when prescribed as a contraceptive.
viva.a: Take 30 mg orally twice weekly on fixed days for the first 12 weeks, followed by 30 mg once weekly thereafter, starting on day 1 of menses.

viva.q: Why is ormeloxifene contraindicated in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?
viva.a: Its central anti-estrogenic action increases gonadotropins, which can trigger the enlargement of multiple follicular cysts and cause ovarian pain.

image.brief: Foil blister card displaying eight small white circular 30 mg ormeloxifene tablets with day-of-the-week markers on a clean surface.

items.summary: A centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used as a non-hormonal therapy for menopausal hot flushes and as an adjunctive antihypertensive.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Centrally acting imidazoline and alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist.
Employed as a non-hormonal pharmaceutical remedy for vasomotor hot flushes.
Trade brand names include Catapres, Arkamin, and Dixarit.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral tablets.
Transdermal patch.
Epidural injection for analgesia.
Intravenous and topical formulations.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Stimulates inhibitory alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem vasomotor centre, blunting peripheral sympathetic outflow.
Reduces systemic peripheral vascular resistance and lowers systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
Narrows the central hypothalamic thermoregulatory set-point window, suppressing the frequency and intensity of vasomotor hot flushes.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Vasomotor hot flushes: Initial dose of 0.025 mg BD orally, titrated upward according to tolerance to 0.075 mg BD.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Non-hormonal relief of hot flushes in postmenopausal women, especially gravidas or women with co-existing hypertension.
Antihypertensive therapy in chronic arterial hypertension.
Adjunctive therapy in psychiatric disorders: anxiety, post-traumatic stress, and sleep disturbances.
Pre-medication procedural sedation and migraine prophylaxis.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and nasal mucosal dryness.
Central nervous system sedation, somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue.
Postural hypotension, headache, anxiety, nausea, vomiting, and constipation.
Peripheral paraesthesia and severe rebound hypertensive crisis upon abrupt cessation.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Pre-existing endogenous depression or severe depressive disorders.
Severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes).
Second- or third-degree atrioventricular heart block.
Recent acute myocardial infarction.
Severe chronic kidney disease and known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What dangerous physiological rebound phenomenon occurs upon abrupt discontinuation of clonidine?
viva.a: Rebound sympathetic storm resulting in acute, life-threatening hypertensive crisis, severe tachycardia, tremors, agitation, and potential intracerebral haemorrhage.

viva.q: What makes clonidine an attractive option for treating menopausal hot flushes in breast cancer survivors?
viva.a: It is completely non-hormonal and does not activate estrogen receptors, making it safe for women with contraindications to systemic hormone replacement therapy.

image.brief: Small blister card of minute 0.025 mg blue clonidine tablets beside an unopened transdermal patch on a neutral examination desk.

items.summary: A synthetic steroid with tissue-specific estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic properties, used for postmenopausal symptoms and osteoporosis prevention.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Synthetic 19-nortestosterone steroid derivative possessing combined estrogenic, progestogenic, and weak androgenic actions.
Marketed internationally as Livial and Tibofem.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Metabolised in vivo into 3-alpha- and 3-beta-hydroxy metabolites that exert estrogenic agonism on the brain, bone, and vaginal epithelium.
Metabolised into a Delta-4 isomer that binds to progesterone and androgen receptors, protecting the endometrium from proliferation.
Inhibits sulfatase enzymes in breast tissue, limiting local estradiol synthesis.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Standard postmenopausal dose: 2.5 mg OD taken orally once daily.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Relief of postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, drenching night sweats).
Prevention of accelerated postmenopausal bone mineral density loss and osteoporotic fractures.
Add-back therapy during prolonged GnRH agonist regimens for endometriosis or fibroids.
Improvement of low sexual libido and mood disturbances in postmenopausal women.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Elevated risk of ischaemic stroke, especially in women aged over 60 years.
Breakthrough vaginal spotting and bleeding, and potential risk of endometrial cancer recurrence.
Abdominal cramping, vaginal candidiasis, mastalgia, and breast tenderness.
Androgenic signs: Mild hirsutism (excess facial hair growth) and weight gain.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Known or previous history of breast carcinoma.
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Active or past history of venous thromboembolism (VTE) or arterial thrombosis.
Active severe liver disease and severe hyperlipidaemia.
Severe cardiac insufficiency, porphyria, and known drug hypersensitivity.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Regular periodic clinical breast examination and screening mammography are essential to detect occult breast lesions.
Must be discontinued at least 4 weeks prior to major elective surgery to minimise the risk of postoperative venous thromboembolism.

viva.q: Why does tibolone not induce endometrial proliferation despite possessing estrogenic activity?
viva.a: Its Delta-4 metabolite exerts strong progestogenic activity on the endometrium and suppresses local sulfatase enzymes, preventing endometrial hyperplasia.

viva.q: What specific health risk identified in the LIFT trial limits tibolone use in women older than 60 years?
viva.a: A significant two-fold increase in the incidence of ischaemic cerebrovascular stroke.

image.brief: Calendar blister packaging showing twenty-eight circular white 2.5 mg tibolone tablets on a wooden clinic consultation surface.

items.summary: An anticholinergic antimuscarinic bladder relaxant used as standard medical therapy for urge urinary incontinence and overactive bladder.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Tertiary amine anticholinergic, antimuscarinic, and direct smooth muscle antispasmodic agent.
Trade preparations include Ditropan, Cystran, Noctorin, and Oxybutin.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Oral tablets and extended-release formulations.
Transdermal gel.
Transdermal patch.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Competitively antagonises muscarinic M1, M2, and M3 cholinergic receptors on the detrusor muscle of the bladder.
Suppresses involuntary detrusor contractions, increasing bladder capacity and diminishing the sensation of urinary urgency.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Oral dose: 2.5 mg OD up to 5 mg TDS/QID.
Transdermal patch: One patch applied twice a week.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Treatment of urge urinary incontinence.
Reduction of excessive daytime and nocturnal micturition frequency.
Suppression of acute debilitating urinary urgency associated with overactive bladder.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Xerostomia (dry mouth and thirst) and dry eyes causing blurred vision.
Anhidrosis with dry pruritic skin and reduced sweating.
Nausea, constipation, dysphagia, drowsiness, dizziness, and headache.
Urinary hesitancy, incomplete bladder emptying, delirium, and confusion.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Untreated narrow-angle glaucoma.
Severe cardiac disease, advanced heart block, and tachyarrhythmias.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and paralytic ileus.
Myasthenia gravis, toxic megacolon, and hyperthyroidism.
Porphyria and known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What is the primary pharmacological action of oxybutynin in managing overactive bladder?
viva.a: It competitively blocks muscarinic M2 and M3 receptors on the detrusor muscle, inhibiting uninhibited contractions and increasing bladder storage capacity.

viva.q: Why does transdermal oxybutynin cause less dry mouth than oral formulations?
viva.a: Transdermal delivery bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism, avoiding high circulating levels of N-desethyloxybutynin, the metabolite responsible for xerostomia.

image.brief: Blister strip of circular 5 mg scored oxybutynin tablets beside a sealed foil transdermal matrix patch on a clinic table.

items.summary: A serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor used for stress urinary incontinence by increasing striated urethral sphincter tone, and for neuropathic pain.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Combined serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI).
Trade names include Cymbalta, Dulotin, Symbal, and Yentreve.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered orally.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Inhibits presynaptic reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) and norepinephrine in Onufs nucleus of the sacral spinal cord.
Augments pudendal somatic nerve stimulation to the striated external urethral sphincter, elevating baseline resting tone.
Enhances dynamic urethral closure pressure to prevent involuntary urine leakage during physical exertion, coughing, or straining.
Increases functional bladder storage capacity.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Stress incontinence: Initial starting dose of 20 mg BD, escalated after 2-4 weeks to 40 mg BD.
Initiation at a lower dose minimises early gastrointestinal and central nervous system side effects.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Moderate to severe female stress urinary incontinence.
Major depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder.
Diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain.
Fibromyalgia and chronic musculoskeletal pain syndromes.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Gastrointestinal: Nausea, dry mouth, diarrhoea, and anorexia.
Central: Insomnia, dizziness, anxiety, restlessness, fatigue, and headache.
Systemic: Blurring of vision, sexual dysfunction, and rare suicidal ideation in young adults.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe hepatic insufficiency.
Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min).
Uncontrolled arterial hypertension.
Pregnancy and lactation.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: How does duloxetine improve symptoms of stress urinary incontinence?
viva.a: It blocks serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake in Onuf's nucleus in the sacral cord, increasing somatic pudendal efferent outflow to contract the external urethral sphincter.

viva.q: What is the single most common side effect that causes patients to discontinue duloxetine therapy early?
viva.a: Severe acute nausea, which can be mitigated by initiating therapy at a reduced dose of 20 mg twice daily with meals.

items.summary: A sterile human plasma-derived immunoglobulin containing antibodies against the Rh(D) antigen, preventing maternal alloimmunisation in Rh-negative gravidas.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Polyclonal human hyperimmune immunoglobulin containing high titres of anti-Rh(D) antibodies.
Derived from screened human donor plasma negative for blood-borne viral pathogens.
Proprietary products include Rhogam, Microgam UF, and Rhophylac (licensed for both IM and IV administration).

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by deep intramuscular injection.
Specific formulations (such as Rhophylac) can be given by intravenous injection.

blocks.title: Mechanism of action
bullets: Binds to fetal Rh(D)-positive red blood cells entering the maternal circulation following fetomaternal haemorrhage.
Promotes immune clearance and destruction of fetal red blood cells in the maternal reticuloendothelial system before B-lymphocytes recognize the D antigen.
Prevents primary maternal immune sensitisation, averting haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) in subsequent pregnancies.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Indian National Guidelines: 50 micrograms for sensitising events prior to 20 weeks gestation; 300 micrograms after 20 weeks and following delivery.
RCOG Guidelines: 250 IU for events prior to 20 weeks gestation; 500 IU after 20 weeks gestation and following delivery.
Must be administered as soon as possible and strictly within 72 hours of any potentially sensitising event or childbirth.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Potentially sensitising obstetric events in non-sensitised Rh-negative women:
Amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS), and fetal blood sampling.
Ectopic pregnancy and molar gestation.
Miscarriage after 12 weeks, or before 12 weeks if accompanied by severe pain, bleeding, or surgical evacuation.
Medical or surgical termination of pregnancy.
Antepartum haemorrhage, external cephalic version (ECV), and blunt abdominal trauma.
Intrauterine fetal demise, manual removal of the placenta, and normal delivery of an Rh-positive neonate within 72 hours.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Local injection site pain, tenderness, erythema, swelling, and mild bruising.
Transient cutaneous allergic rash and pruritus.
Systemic anaphylaxis (extremely rare).

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Documented hypersensitivity to human immunoglobulin preparations.
Pre-existing Rh(D) isoimmunisation with circulating anti-D antibodies (already sensitised mother).

viva.q: What is the mandatory window within which anti-D immunoglobulin must be administered following delivery?
viva.a: It should be administered as soon as possible and within 72 hours of birth, though partial protection is still achieved if given up to 28 days postpartum.

viva.q: What laboratory test is performed after delivery to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage and calculate additional anti-D doses?
viva.a: The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test or flow cytometry, which quantifies fetal red cells in the maternal circulation to adjust anti-D dosage.

items.summary: Recombinant virus-like particle vaccines protecting against high-risk oncogenic HPV types 16 and 18 and benign genital wart types 6 and 11.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Recombinant non-infectious virus-like particle (VLP) subunit vaccines.
Gardasil: Quadrivalent vaccine targeting HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18, manufactured in Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast cells.
Cervarix: Bivalent vaccine targeting oncogenic HPV types 16 and 18, manufactured in baculovirus-infected insect cells.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered by intramuscular injection into the deltoid muscle.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Gardasil schedule: 3-dose regimen at 0, 2, and 6 months, starting from 9 years of age.
Cervarix schedule: 3-dose regimen at 0, 2, and 6 months, starting from 10 years of age.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Gardasil protection: 99% protection against high-grade precancerous cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), anal cancer, vulvar and vaginal cancers, and benign condyloma acuminata (genital warts). Approved for both males and females.
Cervarix protection: 93% protection against HPV-16/18 precancerous cervical lesions and cervical carcinoma. Approved for females.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Local injection site pain, erythema, induration, and swelling.
Systemic: Low-grade fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea, and mild diarrhoea.
Post-vaccination vasovagal syncope (warranting 15 minutes of seated observation).

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis to yeast proteins (Gardasil) or previous vaccine components.
Severe acute febrile illness.
Routine vaccination is generally deferred during confirmed pregnancy.

viva.q: What specific human papillomavirus genotypes are targeted by the quadrivalent Gardasil vaccine?
viva.a: Low-risk types 6 and 11 (causing 90% of genital warts) and high-risk oncogenic types 16 and 18 (causing 70% of cervical cancers).

viva.q: What is the recommended age and standard three-dose schedule for adolescent HPV immunisation?
viva.a: Recommended from 9 to 14 years, administered as a three-dose schedule at 0, 2, and 6 months (or a two-dose schedule at 0 and 6 months before age 15).

items.summary: A 9-valent recombinant virus-like particle vaccine expanding oncogenic coverage to nine HPV genotypes for the prevention of anogenital cancers and warts.

blocks.title: Class and examples
bullets: Nonavalent recombinant virus-like particle (VLP) subunit vaccine.
Stimulates protective neutralising antibodies against 9 distinct HPV genotypes: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.
Proprietary international product is Gardasil 9.

blocks.title: Route
bullets: Administered via intramuscular injection into the deltoid region.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Deltoid intramuscular schedule: 3-dose regimen administered at 0, 2, and 6 months.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Girls and women aged 9-45 years: Prevention of cervical, vulval, and vaginal carcinoma, cervical adenocarcinoma in situ, CIN 1-3, VIN 1-3, VaIN 1-3, and condyloma acuminata.
Girls and women aged 9-26 years: Prevention of anal carcinoma and anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN 1-3).
Boys and men aged 9-26 years: Prevention of genital warts, anal cancer, and AIN 1-3.

blocks.title: Adverse effects
bullets: Local: Deltoid pain, swelling, erythema, and pruritus.
Systemic: Headache, dizziness, fever, and nausea.
Post-vaccine vasovagal syncope and transient seizure-like motor activity (observed for 15 minutes post-injection).
Systemic allergic reactions and rash.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Severe hypersensitivity to yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or any vaccine constituent.
Severe acute febrile illness.
Known drug hypersensitivity.

viva.q: What additional five high-risk oncogenic HPV types are covered by the nonavalent vaccine over the quadrivalent vaccine?
viva.a: Types 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58, which collectively account for an additional 15% to 20% of invasive cervical cancers.

viva.q: Why is a mandatory 15-minute post-vaccination observation period recommended following Gardasil 9?
viva.a: Adolescents have a known predisposition to post-immunisation vasovagal syncope, which can occasionally present with transient seizure-like activity.
